meta.blurb: Four retired friends meet every Wednesday for tea and old crimes. Then the man who wants to sell their garden is found dead in a locked glasshouse, and one alibi mentions a train that Walter, the retired signalman, knows was not running.
meta.bible: Edith Marsh: retired headteacher, sharp and calm, keeps a notebook in her cardigan pocket. Walter Pike: retired railway signalman who knows every timetable. Meera Shah: retired nurse. Fergus Lyle: retired locksmith, gnarled hands, loves a good lock. Together they are the Wednesday Club and meet at three o'clock in the Garden Room with tea and lemon cake. Conrad Vane: the new owner of Maple Court, sharp suit, cold at first, secretly changes his mind and writes a letter on Saturday withdrawing the sale. Harold Stott: Vane's finance manager, round and rosy, polished black shoes, steals money from residents' care fees; the killer. Joe Bell: the gardener for twenty years, gruff and honest; Saturday night at his daughter's house. Lucy Pym: the young cook. Gwen Hartley: eighty-eight, planted all the roses, uses a walking stick, saw a man in a long raincoat at nine. Sergeant Tom Rudd: tall young police officer. Ruth Vane: Conrad's sister, who inherits Maple Court. Maple Court: a brick house turned into flats for older people. Willowby: the small town. Glasshouse: at the end of the garden, full of tomatoes and seedlings; the door locks only from outside with a key; three keys exist: Vane's, Joe's and a spare in the office cabinet with a four-figure code known to Joe, Lucy and Stott. Facts: the pots are bright red clay; on Saturday there was no railway service because of track repairs, only replacement buses, so Stott's six-fifteen train did not exist; Stott signed out of the visitors' book at six; Vane was struck at the back of the head; Vane's letter was hidden in a seed tin; the secret that the pots were pulled down on top of him was told only to Edith. Voice and tone: warm, gently funny and clear, a fair-play puzzle for older readers; the death is stated plainly with no gore; Stott confesses and is arrested. ADDED NAMES AND FACTS FOR THE FULL BOOK: Pat Bell: Joe's daughter, with whom he spends Saturday night; her son Sam, aged ten, plays cards with Joe. Dennis Kemp: a builder of Kemp and Sons who wanted to buy the garden. Ravi Anand: a resident, retired bus conductor. Tilly Drummond: a resident who knits. Mr Greaves: the Willowby stationmaster. Inspector Hale: Sergeant Rudd's senior officer. Nina Doyle: the replacement bus driver in a bright jacket. The Garden Room is where the Wednesday Club meets; the lounge is where residents' meetings are held. The back gate: a green gate at the bottom of the garden that opens from the lane with a simple latch. Stott's long fawn raincoat, worn at the fair although the sky was blue. Stott's silver car. Vane's key was found in his own jacket pocket. Timeline: the fair is on Saturday; Vane is found on Sunday morning; the trap meeting is on a Thursday morning, about three and a half weeks after. Vane saw Gwen's care-fee statement at the fair and asked Stott to meet him in the Glasshouse at nine with the account books; he meant to tell Stott the sale was off and the police would be told on Monday.
chapters: A Letter in the Seed Tin

beats.scene: A tall brick house with a long garden and a glasshouse at the end
beats.summary: Maple Court is a tall old house in the small town of Willowby, turned into flats for older people.

beats.scene: A long garden with a rose walk, vegetable beds and a far glasshouse
beats.summary: Behind the house lies a garden with a rose walk, vegetable beds and a Glasshouse full of tomatoes.

beats.scene: Joe Bell the gardener pushes a wheelbarrow along the rose walk
beats.summary: Joe Bell, the gruff gardener who has looked after the garden for twenty years, is introduced.

beats.scene: Gwen Hartley leans on her walking stick and smells a pink rose
beats.summary: Gwen Hartley, aged eighty-eight, planted every rose in the garden and talks to them.

beats.scene: Lucy Pym, the young cook, lifts a golden lemon cake out of the oven
beats.summary: Lucy Pym is the young cook whose lemon cake is famous all over Willowby.

beats.scene: Four armchairs, a tea tray and a newspaper puzzle in a bright shabby room
beats.summary: Every Wednesday at three four friends meet in the Garden Room with tea and cake.

beats.scene: Edith Marsh with glasses on her nose writes in a small notebook
beats.summary: Edith Marsh, a retired headteacher, is calm and sharp and keeps a notebook in her pocket.

beats.scene: Walter Pike in an old station cap beside a shelf of railway timetables
beats.summary: Walter Pike, a retired railway signalman, knows every timetable in the county.

beats.scene: Meera Shah pours tea with a calm smile and a steady hand
beats.summary: Meera Shah, a retired nurse, notices small things about people that others miss.

beats.scene: Fergus Lyle holds a brass lock in his gnarled hands
beats.summary: Fergus Lyle, a retired locksmith, loves a good lock and has made and mended them for fifty years.

beats.scene: A table of newspaper cuttings, a teapot and four serious faces
beats.summary: One Wednesday the club studies an old newspaper story about a silver cup stolen from a seaside hotel.

beats.scene: Fergus points at a drawing of a hotel safe while Walter checks a timetable
beats.summary: Fergus and Walter solve the old case in their own ways, and Edith writes down the answer.

beats.scene: A black car stops on the gravel and Mr Vane steps out
beats.summary: On Monday the new owner, Mr Conrad Vane, arrives with his finance manager Harold Stott.

beats.scene: Mr Vane pins a white notice to the board in the hall
beats.summary: Mr Conrad Vane pins a notice saying that the garden will be sold to builders.

beats.scene: Gwen Hartley waves her walking stick at the notice in the hall
beats.summary: Gwen Hartley protests that she planted every rose in the garden with her own hands.

beats.scene: Mr Vane stands stiffly in the hall with his hands behind his back
beats.summary: Mr Vane answers coldly that business is business and that roses can be planted anywhere.

beats.scene: Joe Bell shakes a fist at Mr Vane beside his wheelbarrow
beats.summary: Joe Bell shouts at Mr Vane that he will lose his job together with the garden.

beats.scene: Edith watches Mr Vane look down the long garden toward the glasshouse
beats.summary: Edith notices that Mr Vane looks sad, not cold, when he stares at the Glasshouse.

beats.scene: The four friends around the Garden Room table writing a list
beats.summary: The club meets in a hurry and agrees to write a petition against the sale.

beats.scene: Mr Vane stands in the lounge beside Harold Stott, who holds a briefcase
beats.summary: On Friday Mr Vane tells the residents the sale is final while Stott smiles beside him.

beats.scene: Stalls, flags and bunting on a sunny lawn
beats.summary: On Saturday the summer fair fills the lawn with stalls, flags and a brass band.

beats.scene: Gwen sells seedlings and roses while Joe hammers a tent peg
beats.summary: Gwen runs a stall of seedlings and cut roses while Joe puts up the tents, still angry.

beats.scene: Walter shows Fergus a leaflet at the cake stall, frowning
beats.summary: At the cake stall Walter grumbles that the railway is closed all weekend and buses run instead.

beats.scene: Mr Vane stops beside Gwen's rose stall and looks at a pink rose
beats.summary: Mr Vane walks round the fair alone and stops at Gwen's stall.

beats.scene: Gwen hands Mr Vane a crumpled bank paper and he reads it, frowning
beats.summary: Gwen gives Mr Vane a crumpled paper from her bank that she cannot understand, and he keeps it.

beats.scene: Mr Vane writes at the potting bench while Meera watches through the glass
beats.summary: Meera sees Mr Vane alone in the Glasshouse, writing at the potting bench.

beats.scene: Mr Vane speaks quietly to Lucy at the cake stall
beats.summary: Mr Vane tells Lucy he has a meeting in the Glasshouse at nine and must not be disturbed.

beats.scene: Harold Stott with a fawn raincoat over his arm looks at a blue sky
beats.summary: Stott carries a long raincoat although the sky is blue, and Edith notices.

beats.scene: Stott checks his watch in the tea tent and speaks to Edith
beats.summary: Stott tells Edith he must leave early to catch the six-fifteen train to London.

beats.scene: Stott signs the visitors' book in the front hall with a flourish
beats.summary: At six o'clock Stott signs out in the visitors' book with a flourish and leaves.

beats.scene: Joe puts tools away as the tents come down and the sun sinks
beats.summary: The fair ends, and Joe puts away his tools and leaves to spend the night at his daughter Pat's house.

beats.scene: Lucy carries a covered tray along the corridor
beats.summary: Lucy serves supper, and the dinner she leaves out for Mr Vane stays untouched.

beats.scene: The four friends in the Garden Room as the sun goes down
beats.summary: In the evening the four friends talk about how strangely Mr Vane has behaved.

beats.scene: Gwen with a tray of seedlings walks the dusky garden path
beats.summary: At nine o'clock Gwen goes out to fetch her unsold seedlings from a bench by the Glasshouse.

beats.scene: A lit glasshouse at dusk with a man in a long raincoat inside
beats.summary: Gwen sees a light in the Glasshouse and a man in a long raincoat inside.

beats.scene: Gwen turns back along the path, leaving her seedlings behind
beats.summary: Gwen does not want to disturb the man and goes back to bed.

beats.scene: Maple Court asleep under a full moon with every window dark
beats.summary: The night passes quietly while the Glasshouse lamp burns on alone.

beats.scene: Joe walks up the lane at dawn with his cap in his hand
beats.summary: On Sunday morning Joe comes back early to water the tomatoes.

beats.scene: Joe turns a key in the glasshouse door and stops
beats.summary: Joe finds the Glasshouse locked, opens it with his key and finds Mr Vane on the floor.

beats.scene: Joe runs across the lawn toward the house, waving his arms
beats.summary: Joe runs to the house and telephones the police.

beats.scene: Sergeant Tom Rudd, tall and young, steps out of a police car
beats.summary: Sergeant Tom Rudd arrives, tall and young and careful, and asks Joe what he found.

beats.scene: The doctor kneels beside Mr Vane while the sergeant writes
beats.summary: A doctor examines Mr Vane while Sergeant Rudd looks around the Glasshouse.

beats.scene: Rudd and the doctor stand in the glasshouse talking quietly
beats.summary: The doctor and Rudd decide that Mr Vane slipped and fell, and the case is closed.

beats.scene: Residents in dressing gowns listen in the lounge as the sergeant speaks
beats.summary: The residents are told that Mr Vane has died in an accident.

beats.scene: A grey van drives slowly down the drive between the rose beds
beats.summary: Mr Vane is taken away and the house falls silent; Rudd telephones his sister Ruth.

beats.scene: Edith stands alone at the glasshouse door holding her notebook
beats.summary: In the afternoon Edith walks to the Glasshouse and stares at its door and lamp.

beats.scene: Four friends in the Garden Room with an empty cake plate
beats.summary: That evening the club meets without cake, and Edith says she does not believe it was an accident.

beats.scene: Edith counts points on her fingers while the others listen
beats.summary: Edith lists what troubles her: a missed supper, a lonely night in the Glasshouse and a lamp left burning.

beats.scene: Walter shakes his head and taps the table with one finger
beats.summary: Walter says a verdict made before lunch on a Sunday is a verdict made in a hurry.

beats.scene: Four friends lean over the table with their hands on Edith's notebook
beats.summary: The club decides to look into Mr Vane's death quietly, and Fergus will start with the lock.

beats.scene: Fergus kneels at the glasshouse door and runs a finger over its lock
beats.summary: On Monday morning Fergus studies the Glasshouse lock while his friends watch.

beats.scene: Fergus holds up one finger and points at the keyhole
beats.summary: Fergus explains that the Glasshouse door can only be locked from outside, with a key.

beats.scene: The friends frown at the door as the truth sinks in
beats.summary: They realise that someone locked the door after Mr Vane was already inside.

beats.scene: Joe holds up his own glasshouse key on a loop of string
beats.summary: Joe tells them that only three keys fit: Mr Vane's, his own and a spare in the office.

beats.scene: A grey steel cabinet with a numbered keypad hangs on the office wall
beats.summary: The spare key is locked in an office cabinet that opens only with a four-figure code.

beats.scene: Edith draws three keys in her notebook with a question mark beside each
beats.summary: Edith writes down the three keys and wonders which one the door-locker used.

beats.scene: Meera describes what she saw as the stretcher passed
beats.summary: Meera tells the others what she glimpsed on the stretcher: a wound at the back of the head.

beats.scene: Meera tips gently forward in her chair to show how a fall works
beats.summary: Meera explains that a man who fell on his face could not hurt the back of his head.

beats.scene: Edith speaks quietly to Sergeant Rudd on the front steps of Maple Court
beats.summary: Edith tells Rudd about the lock and the wound and asks him to keep the case open.

beats.scene: Rudd glances around and speaks quietly with a hand beside his mouth
beats.summary: Rudd secretly tells Edith that a shelf of pots had been pulled down on Mr Vane, and asks her to tell nobody.

beats.scene: Joe sits in a potting shed with a mug, frowning at his boots
beats.summary: The club visits Joe in his potting shed, and he admits the quarrel with Mr Vane.

beats.scene: Joe's daughter Pat and her son Sam play cards at a kitchen table
beats.summary: Joe says he spent Saturday night at his daughter Pat's house, playing cards with her son Sam.

beats.scene: Joe holds a rose cutting in his rough hands
beats.summary: Joe says he would never harm a living thing in the garden, and Edith believes him.

beats.scene: Joe taps a chain of keys hanging from his belt
beats.summary: Joe says his key never left his belt chain and that Mr Vane meant to look after the Glasshouse himself.

beats.scene: Gwen in a flowered armchair points toward the glasshouse window
beats.summary: Gwen tells the friends about the light and the man in the long raincoat.

beats.scene: A man in a long raincoat with his collar turned up, seen from behind
beats.summary: Gwen could not see the man's face, only a long raincoat with a turned-up collar.

beats.scene: Edith writes raincoat in her notebook and underlines it twice
beats.summary: Edith notes that nobody wears a raincoat on a warm dry evening unless he wants to hide something.

beats.scene: Lucy stands in the kitchen holding a tray with an untouched dinner
beats.summary: Lucy shows the untouched dinner tray and says Mr Vane told her about a meeting at nine.

beats.scene: Lucy twists a dish towel and shakes her head
beats.summary: Lucy does not know whom Mr Vane was meeting; he seemed tired but oddly cheerful.

beats.scene: Edith's notebook open at a page headed with one question
beats.summary: Edith writes the question: whom did Mr Vane mean to meet at nine, and who knew?

beats.scene: The visitors' book lies open on the hall desk, a finger on a name
beats.summary: The visitors' book shows that only Harold Stott signed out on Saturday evening.

beats.scene: Harold Stott's neat signature with a big flourish and the time beside it
beats.summary: Stott's name is written with a flourish and the time, six o'clock exactly, beside it.

beats.scene: Stott's tidy office with a polished desk and a brass pen
beats.summary: The friends visit Harold Stott in his very tidy manager's office.

beats.scene: Stott sits with a polite, sad expression and folded hands
beats.summary: Stott tells them he left at six, caught the train to London and heard the news only on Monday.

beats.scene: Stott spreads his hands as he talks about the sale
beats.summary: Stott says that the sale must still go ahead and that one must be practical.

beats.scene: Edith holds her teacup and asks a gentle question
beats.summary: Edith asks gentle questions about the journey, and Stott answers each one too quickly.

beats.scene: Fergus admires a grey steel cabinet in the estate office
beats.summary: Fergus asks Stott about the key cabinet, and Stott says he hardly ever touches it.

beats.scene: Walter stands on the office steps scratching his head
beats.summary: Outside, Walter is troubled by the six-fifteen train but cannot say why.

beats.scene: Walter drops his spoon over a bowl of soup in the dining room
beats.summary: At lunch the next day Walter remembers that no trains ran on Saturday.

beats.scene: Edith's notebook page with Stott's name and a question mark beside it
beats.summary: Edith writes Stott's name with a question mark but reminds the club a mistake is not proof.

beats.scene: Rudd unlocks the glasshouse door while the four friends wait
beats.summary: On Wednesday Sergeant Rudd lets the club into the Glasshouse as long as they touch nothing.

beats.scene: Warm green air, tomato plants and seedling trays inside the glasshouse
beats.summary: Inside, the Glasshouse is warm and green, with tomatoes, seedling trays and a potting bench.

beats.scene: Fergus kneels at the door, studying fresh scratches around the keyhole
beats.summary: Fergus finds fresh scratches around the keyhole on the outside of the lock.

beats.scene: Walter points at a gap on a shelf of bright red clay pots
beats.summary: Walter notices the red clay pots, a gap on the top shelf and a bucket of broken pieces.

beats.scene: Joe stands in the doorway nodding at the red pots
beats.summary: Joe says the red clay pots never leave the Glasshouse, and the garden paths are grey gravel.

beats.scene: A small seed tin sits on the potting bench among neat labelled boxes
beats.summary: Edith notices a seed tin on the potting bench that does not belong among the labelled boxes.

beats.scene: Edith opens a seed tin and finds a letter under the tomato seed packets
beats.summary: Under the tomato seed packets in the tin, Edith finds a folded letter.

beats.scene: Edith holds the letter up to the light from the glass roof
beats.summary: The letter, dated Saturday and signed Conrad Vane, says he has decided not to sell the garden.

beats.scene: Walter and Meera read the letter over Edith's shoulders
beats.summary: Walter points out that Mr Vane changed his mind on the very day he died.

beats.scene: Sergeant Rudd slips the letter into a clear plastic bag
beats.summary: Rudd bags the letter as evidence, and Edith asks who else knew Mr Vane had changed his mind.

beats.scene: Stott pins a new notice to the hall board while residents watch
beats.summary: Next morning Stott pins a notice saying the sale will go ahead in spite of Mr Vane's death.

beats.scene: Angry residents crowd round the board while Gwen taps her stick
beats.summary: The residents crowd round the notice, angry and worried.

beats.scene: Edith reads the notice with her pencil against her lip
beats.summary: Edith wonders who knew Mr Vane had changed his mind, since Stott's notice suggests he did not.

beats.scene: A grey car arrives and a tired woman in a dark coat steps out
beats.summary: Ruth Vane, Conrad's sister, arrives at Maple Court after a long drive.

beats.scene: Ruth Vane walks slowly beside Edith along the rose walk
beats.summary: Ruth tells Edith she had not spoken to Conrad for a year, and the roses make her cry.

beats.scene: Dennis Kemp, a heavy man with rolled plans, strides into the hall
beats.summary: Dennis Kemp, the builder, arrives with rolled plans and demands to see Mr Stott.

beats.scene: Kemp wags a finger at Stott in the hall with plans under his arm
beats.summary: Fergus overhears Kemp saying that his money was ready and the garden was promised to him.

beats.scene: Edith adds two names to a list in her notebook
beats.summary: Edith adds Kemp, who would lose if the garden were saved, and Ruth, who inherits.

beats.scene: Edith draws a table of who wanted what and who had keys
beats.summary: Edith lists who wanted the sale, who wanted it stopped and who could reach a key.

beats.scene: The four friends raise teacups around the table in the Garden Room
beats.summary: At the next meeting the club votes to go on, and Lucy brings the lemon cake.

beats.scene: Meera sits beside Gwen holding a bank statement under a lamp
beats.summary: Meera helps Gwen read her monthly bank statement of care fees.

beats.scene: Meera's finger rests on two lines of the same fee on the statement
beats.summary: Meera sees that Gwen is charged her care fee twice each month.

beats.scene: Gwen shakes her head in surprise over a cup of tea
beats.summary: Gwen thought that was how care fees worked; Meera says the contract names one fee.

beats.scene: Meera and Fergus go from door to door with a notebook
beats.summary: Meera and Fergus knock on doors and ask residents to show their statements.

beats.scene: Ravi Anand and Tilly Drummond show their statements at their doors
beats.summary: Mr Anand and Mrs Drummond show their statements, and both are charged twice as well.

beats.scene: A list of eleven names with ticks beside them in Meera's notebook
beats.summary: Eleven residents have been paying the same hidden fee twice every month.

beats.scene: A calendar of twelve months, each marked with the same small cross
beats.summary: The double charge began about a year ago, when the new company took over the accounts.

beats.scene: Edith sits with her notebook and pencil while Meera explains
beats.summary: Edith says that somebody is taking the money and that the finance manager controls the billing.

beats.scene: Gwen taps her stick and speaks about Mr Vane at the fair
beats.summary: Gwen reminds them that Mr Vane took her crumpled paper at the fair and went quiet.

beats.scene: Edith underlines two words in her notebook
beats.summary: Edith concludes that Mr Vane probably understood the extra fees on Saturday, the day he changed his mind.

beats.scene: Edith watches Harold Stott cross the hall in gleaming black shoes
beats.summary: Edith sees a thin line of red dust on Stott's polished shoes.

beats.scene: Stott polishes his shoes with a brush and a tin of black wax
beats.summary: Everyone knows that Stott polishes his shoes daily, so the dust must be recent.

beats.scene: Edith with a teacup asks Stott a casual question in the hall
beats.summary: Edith asks Stott whether he has been in the garden, and he says not since the fair.

beats.scene: Edith stands on the grey gravel path looking at the ground
beats.summary: Edith checks the garden paths and finds only grey gravel, with no red dust anywhere.

beats.scene: Walter stands at Willowby station reading a notice board
beats.summary: Walter walks to the railway station to see the notice board for himself.

beats.scene: Mr Greaves the stationmaster points at the yellow poster
beats.summary: The stationmaster, Mr Greaves, confirms that no train ran on Saturday, only buses.

beats.scene: A bus timetable pinned inside the stationmaster's office door
beats.summary: The only replacement bus that evening left the station at twenty past six.

beats.scene: A bus driver in a yellow jacket shakes her head beside her bus
beats.summary: The replacement bus driver, Nina Doyle, does not remember a man like Stott among her six passengers.

beats.scene: Walter writes on the back of a bus ticket as he walks home
beats.summary: Walter writes down all he has learned and decides that Stott either made a mistake or lied.

beats.scene: Walter slaps a bus ticket on the table in the Garden Room
beats.summary: Edith says that Stott lied about the train, perhaps because he never left Maple Court.

beats.scene: Fergus and Joe stand before the grey cabinet in the estate office
beats.summary: Fergus asks to look closely at the spare key and its cabinet, with the sergeant's permission.

beats.scene: Fergus examines the worn keypad buttons close up with his lens
beats.summary: Fergus notices that four buttons of the keypad are more worn than the rest.

beats.scene: Fergus holds the key tag up to the light and finds red dust
beats.summary: Fergus finds red clay dust on the tag and ring of the spare Glasshouse key.

beats.scene: Fergus draws a conclusion with the key in his white-gloved hand
beats.summary: Fergus explains that the key was handled by someone with red clay on his hands and put back.

beats.scene: Lucy points at four numbers on the keypad in the estate office
beats.summary: Lucy says that only Stott, Joe and she know the cabinet's code.

beats.scene: Lucy sits in the kitchen with a glass of water
beats.summary: Lucy swears she did not take the key; she served supper and then sat with the residents.

beats.scene: Joe scratches his head by the grey cabinet, thinking
beats.summary: Joe says he had no reason to touch the cabinet on Saturday and was at his daughter's.

beats.scene: Edith crosses names off a list, leaving only Stott
beats.summary: With Lucy and Joe accounted for, only Stott could have used the code that night.

beats.scene: A green gate at the bottom of the garden with a simple latch
beats.summary: Fergus finds the green back gate that opens from the lane with a simple latch.

beats.scene: Edith looks at the glasshouse from the green gate at dusk
beats.summary: Edith sees that Stott could have slipped in unseen, but they still have no proof.

beats.scene: Sergeant Rudd sits among the four friends with a slice of lemon cake
beats.summary: At the next Wednesday meeting Sergeant Rudd joins the club for tea.

beats.scene: Edith counts the clues on her fingers in front of Rudd
beats.summary: Edith lays out the lie about the train, the red dust, the double fees, the key and the raincoat.

beats.scene: Rudd shakes his head slowly with his plate empty on his knee
beats.summary: Rudd says that red dust, lies and a forgetful driver are not proof.

beats.scene: Sergeant Rudd sighs beside a plate of lemon cake
beats.summary: Rudd explains that Inspector Hale thinks the case is closed and wants more than suspicion.

beats.scene: Rudd leans forward and speaks quietly across the tea table
beats.summary: Rudd says he needs Stott to say something only the killer would know.

beats.scene: Edith looks quietly at her notebook, thinking of the secret
beats.summary: Edith thinks of the one thing only the killer would know: the shelf of pots she has promised to keep secret.

beats.scene: A calendar with Thursday morning circled in pencil
beats.summary: Edith proposes a trap: a residents' meeting on Thursday morning with Stott speaking.

beats.scene: Edith draws a plan with four small circles and a cross
beats.summary: Edith draws her plan: four circles for the friends and a cross for Stott.

beats.scene: Rudd points to the next room on the plan
beats.summary: Rudd will wait in the next room with the door ajar; Joe will stand at the back.

beats.scene: Edith sits awake at her window with a cup of mint tea
beats.summary: That night Edith cannot sleep but feels ready.

beats.scene: Chairs set out in rows in the Garden Room like a small meeting
beats.summary: On Wednesday afternoon the friends set out chairs in the Garden Room to rehearse the meeting.

beats.scene: Walter practises his speech from a card, frowning
beats.summary: Walter practises his part about the train, but it is far too long, and Edith trims it.

beats.scene: Meera reads aloud from a list of figures with a clipboard
beats.summary: Meera practises explaining the double fees in a calm voice, holding the statements.

beats.scene: Fergus drops a key on the carpet and everyone laughs
beats.summary: Fergus practises holding up a stand-in key and drops it, and everyone laughs.

beats.scene: Gwen sits at the front with her stick across her knees
beats.summary: Gwen insists on a front seat and says her stick will tap if she hears a lie.

beats.scene: Lucy takes a golden lemon cake out of the oven
beats.summary: Lucy bakes a lemon cake for the meeting without being asked.

beats.scene: Ruth Vane sits beside Gwen in the front row
beats.summary: Ruth Vane agrees to come and sit beside Gwen in the front row.

beats.scene: Joe stands at the back of the empty lounge with his arms folded
beats.summary: Joe grumbles that he is not an actor but agrees to stand at the back and say nothing.

beats.scene: Stott picks up Edith's notebook from a table in the hall
beats.summary: Stott picks up Edith's notebook, and she tells him it is only a shopping list.

beats.scene: Edith stands in the moonlit doorway of the glasshouse
beats.summary: On the night before the meeting Edith stands at the Glasshouse door and feels steady.

beats.scene: The lounge fills with residents, a tea trolley and rows of chairs
beats.summary: On Thursday morning the lounge fills with residents, and Lucy's lemon cake waits on a table.

beats.scene: Harold Stott arrives with a briefcase and a smile, his shoes shining
beats.summary: Stott arrives, smiling and confident, to speak to the residents.

beats.scene: Sergeant Rudd slips into the next room and leaves the door ajar
beats.summary: Rudd waits in the next room with the door open a crack.

beats.scene: Harold Stott speaks to a restless crowd with his hands spread wide
beats.summary: Stott tells the meeting that the sale of the garden must go ahead.

beats.scene: The residents groan while Gwen grips her stick and keeps it still
beats.summary: The residents groan, and Gwen holds her stick still as promised.

beats.scene: Edith rises from the second row with her notebook in her hand
beats.summary: Edith asks whether she may say a few words, and Stott graciously agrees.

beats.scene: Edith speaks gently to a quiet room, her notebook closed in her hand
beats.summary: Edith tells the meeting plainly that Mr Vane was found dead in the Glasshouse after a fall.

beats.scene: Harold Stott frowns with his mouth open, a flowerpot on the table behind him
beats.summary: Stott slips: he sighs about poor Mr Vane lying under all those pots that someone pulled down.

beats.scene: Gwen's stick strikes the floor once in a silent room
beats.summary: Silence falls, and Gwen taps her stick once, as agreed.

beats.scene: Edith points calmly at Harold Stott across the chairs
beats.summary: Edith asks Stott how he knows the pots were pulled down when nobody has been told.

beats.scene: Stott goes pale, loosening his collar with one finger
beats.summary: Stott goes pale and says that Joe must have told him.

A1A2: Maple Court was a tall old house at the edge of Willowby.
Behind the house there was a long garden full of roses.
Joe Bell was the gardener, and he had worked there for twenty years.
Gwen Hartley was eighty-eight years old, and she had planted all the roses.
Lucy Pym was the young cook, and her lemon cake was famous.
Every Wednesday at three, four friends met in the Garden Room.
Edith Marsh was a retired teacher with a small notebook.
Walter Pike had worked on the railway and knew every timetable.
Meera Shah was a retired nurse with a calm, kind smile.
Fergus Lyle had made and fixed locks for fifty years.
The friends read about an old crime in the newspaper.
Fergus knew the lock, Walter knew the train, and they solved it.
On Monday a long black car stopped outside the house.
Mr Vane pinned a notice on the board in the hall.
Gwen Hartley waved her stick and said she had planted every rose.
Mr Vane said coldly that roses could grow somewhere else.
Joe Bell shouted that he would lose his job too.
Edith saw that Mr Vane looked sad when he saw the garden.
The friends wrote a letter and asked everyone to sign it.
On Friday Mr Vane told everyone that the sale was final.
On Saturday the garden held a summer fair.
Gwen sold small plants, and Joe put up the tents.
Walter said that the trains were not running that weekend.
Mr Vane came to the fair and stopped at Gwen's stall.
Gwen gave Mr Vane a bank paper, and he read it carefully.
Later Meera saw Mr Vane writing alone in the glasshouse.
Mr Vane told Lucy that he had a meeting at nine.
Mr Stott carried a long coat on a sunny day.

At six o'clock Mr Stott signed his name and left.
Joe put away his tools and left for his daughter's house.
Lucy made supper, but Mr Vane did not come to eat.
The four friends sat together and talked about Mr Vane.
At nine o'clock Gwen went to get her small plants.
Gwen saw a light and a man in a long coat.
Gwen did not want to disturb him, so she went back.
The house was quiet, and the lamp burned all night.

Joe opened the locked door and saw Mr Vane on the floor.
Joe ran to the house and called the police.
A police car came, and Sergeant Tom Rudd got out of it.
A doctor looked at Mr Vane while the sergeant looked around.
They said that Mr Vane had slipped and fallen.
The sergeant told the residents that Mr Vane had died.
A van took Mr Vane away, and the house was quiet.
In the afternoon Edith walked to the glasshouse alone.
That evening the four friends met, but nobody wanted cake.
Edith said that a man does not fall without a reason.
Walter said that the police had decided too fast.
They agreed to look into the matter quietly together.
On Monday Fergus looked closely at the lock on the glasshouse door.
Fergus said that the door locked only from the outside.
Someone had locked the door after Mr Vane was inside.
Joe said that only three keys fitted the lock.
The third key was in a box with a number lock.
Edith wrote down the three keys and wondered which one was used.
Meera said that she saw a mark on the back of his head.
Meera said that a man who falls forward hurts his front.
Edith told Sergeant Rudd about the lock and the mark.
The sergeant whispered a secret to Edith and asked for silence.
The friends visited Joe in his shed, and he looked worried.
Joe said he spent Saturday night at his daughter's house.
Joe said that he would never hurt the garden or its people.
Joe kept his key on his belt all through the weekend.
Gwen told the friends about a light in the glasshouse.
She saw only his long coat and the back of his head.
Edith said that nobody wore a long coat on a warm night.
Lucy showed the friends Mr Vane's dinner, which nobody had eaten.
Lucy did not know who he was going to meet.
Edith wrote down one question: who did he meet?
Edith read the visitors' book, and only one name was there.
Mr Stott had signed his name at six o'clock exactly.
The friends visited Mr Stott in his tidy office.
Mr Stott said he had left at six and heard the news later.
Mr Stott said that the sale would still go ahead.
Edith asked about his journey, and he answered very quickly.
Fergus asked about the key box, and Mr Stott smiled.
Walter felt that the six-fifteen train was wrong somehow.
At lunch Walter remembered that no trains ran on Saturday.
Edith wrote Mr Stott's name in her notebook with a question mark.
Sergeant Rudd opened the glasshouse door for the four friends.
Inside, the glasshouse was warm and full of green plants.
Fergus found new scratches on the metal around the lock.
Walter saw a gap on the shelf of red clay pots.
Joe said that the red pots never left the glasshouse.
Edith saw a small tin on the bench that looked wrong.
Under the seed packets Edith found a folded letter.
In the letter Mr Vane said he would not sell the garden.
Walter said that Mr Vane had changed his mind that day.
The sergeant put the letter in a bag and locked it away.
Mr Stott pinned a new notice about the sale on the board.
The residents read the notice and were angry.
Edith wondered who knew that Mr Vane had changed his mind.
Mr Vane's sister came to Maple Court in a grey car.
Ruth walked with Edith and said she missed her brother.
A builder named Dennis Kemp came with big rolled plans.
Mr Kemp said that Mr Stott had promised him the garden.
Edith put two more names on her list: Kemp and Ruth.
Edith wrote who wanted the sale and who wanted to stop it.
The friends decided to keep going, with tea and cake.
Meera sat with Gwen and helped her read a bank letter.
Meera saw the same fee twice in each month.
Gwen thought that this was how care fees worked.
Meera and Fergus asked other residents to show their papers.
Mr Anand and Mrs Drummond had the same two lines.
In the end eleven people had the same extra fee.
The extra fee had been charged for about a year.
Edith said someone was taking money from the residents.
Gwen said Mr Vane had read her paper and become quiet.
Edith thought Mr Vane learned about the fees on Saturday.
Edith saw red dust on Mr Stott's shiny black shoes.
Mr Stott cleaned his shoes every day, so the dust was new.
Mr Stott said he had not been near the garden.
Edith walked the paths and found only grey gravel.
Walter went to the station to read the notice board.
Mr Greaves said that no trains ran on Saturday.
The replacement bus left at twenty past six.
The bus driver did not remember a man like Mr Stott.
Walter wrote down all that he had learned that day.
Edith said that Mr Stott had lied about the train.
Fergus asked to look at the spare key.
Fergus saw that four buttons were more worn than the rest.
Fergus found red dust on the tag of the spare key.
The spare key had been used near the red pots.
Lucy said only three people knew the code.
Lucy said that she had not taken the key.
Joe had not opened the cabinet on Saturday at all.
Only Mr Stott could have used the code that night.
Fergus found a green gate at the bottom of the garden.
Edith knew they still had no proof of anything.
Sergeant Rudd came to tea with the friends.
Edith told the sergeant everything the friends had found.
Sergeant Rudd said that these facts were not proof.
Inspector Hale thought that the case was closed.
The sergeant needed Mr Stott to say something only the killer knew.
Edith knew one secret that only the killer would know.
Edith planned a big meeting of the residents for Thursday morning.
Edith drew a plan with four circles and one cross.
Rudd would wait in the next room with the door open.
That night Edith could not sleep and drank mint tea.
The friends put out chairs and practised the meeting.
Walter's speech about the train was far too long.
Meera practised the part about the extra fees in a calm voice.
Fergus dropped the key on the floor, and the others laughed.
Gwen wanted a seat at the front of the room.
Lucy baked a lemon cake for the meeting.
Ruth agreed to sit with Gwen at the meeting.
Joe agreed to stand at the back and say nothing.
Mr Stott asked about Edith's notebook, and she smiled.
On the last night Edith stood at the glasshouse door.
On Thursday morning the lounge filled with people.
Mr Stott came in with a big smile on his face.
Sergeant Rudd waited in the next room with the door open.
Mr Stott told everyone that the sale must go on.
The residents were unhappy, but Gwen kept her stick still.
Edith stood up and asked to say a few words.
Edith said that Mr Vane died after a fall.
Mr Stott said that Mr Vane lay under all the pots.
Gwen tapped her stick once in the silent room.
Edith asked how he knew about the pots.
Mr Stott said that Joe had told him.
Joe said from the back that he told nobody.
Lucy said she had never seen the pots.
Walter stood up and said no trains ran on Saturday.
Mr Stott said he must have taken the bus.
Walter said the driver did not remember Mr Stott.
Meera told everyone that eleven people paid the fee twice.
Mr Stott said it was only a small mistake.
Fergus held up the spare key with red dust on it.
Mr Stott looked at every face, and his own face fell.
Mr Stott sat down and put his head in his hands.
He said he had taken the money from the residents.
Mr Vane found out about it at the fair.
Mr Stott said he waited in his car until it was dark.
He came back by the green gate and took the spare key.
Mr Vane said that the police would hear of it on Monday.
He said he had hit Mr Vane once, and Mr Vane fell.
Then he made the pots fall to look like an accident.
He locked the door and put the key back.
Nobody in the room spoke, and Edith felt only sadness.
Sergeant Rudd came in and took Mr Stott's arm.
Mr Stott walked out of the house with the police.
The sergeant thanked the Wednesday Club for their help.
The police found the account books in his car.
In the end every resident was paid back in full.
The residents opened letters and smiled with joy.
Ruth Vane read her brother's letter and cried.
Ruth signed a paper, and the garden was saved.
Joe kept his job, and Ruth gave him a fine new gift.
Gwen planted a new rose in memory of Mr Vane.
On Sunday everyone gathered to remember Mr Vane.
Ruth and Joe planted new seeds in the glasshouse.
The four friends were tired, but they were very happy.
Edith opened a new notebook and began to write.
Lucy brought a lemon cake with a candle.
Sergeant Rudd came with cakes and a folder.
The folder held a new puzzle about a lost book.
Each friend took a part in the new puzzle.

B1B2: Maple Court was a tall brick house at the edge of the small town of Willowby. Long ago it had been turned into comfortable flats for older people.
Behind the house lay a long garden with a rose walk, a vegetable patch and a glasshouse at the far end. Every resident had a favourite corner, and most of them could be found there on a sunny day.
Joe Bell had been the gardener at Maple Court for twenty years. He spoke very little, grumbled about the weather, and knew the name of every plant.
Gwen Hartley was eighty-eight years old and walked with a stick. She had planted every rose along the path herself, and she knew each one by its name.
Lucy Pym was the young cook at Maple Court, and she was only twenty-three. Her lemon cake was so good that people in other towns had heard of it.
Every Wednesday at three o'clock, four friends gathered in the Garden Room at the back of the house. They called themselves the Wednesday Club, and they never missed a meeting.
Edith Marsh had been a headteacher for thirty years, and she could tell at once when someone was lying. She kept a small notebook in her cardigan pocket and wrote down everything that puzzled her.
Walter Pike had spent forty years in a railway signal box, and he still knew the timetable of every train in the county. He could not bear a late train, even when he was not on it.
Meera Shah had been a nurse for forty years, and nothing could shock her. She noticed small things about people, such as a pale face or a shaking hand, before they noticed them themselves.
Fergus Lyle had made and mended locks for fifty years, and his old hands were as gnarled as tree roots. He believed that every lock had its own character, and that a good one deserved respect.

That Wednesday the friends were studying an old newspaper story about a silver cup stolen from a seaside hotel. Edith had cut it out and pinned it to a board, and the others took their places around it.

Fergus said that the hotel safe could not be opened without its key, and Walter noticed that the thief's train had never run. Edith wrote the answer in her notebook, and the cake was cut in celebration.

On Monday morning a long black car rolled up the drive and stopped on the gravel. A man in a sharp grey suit stepped out, followed by his finance manager, Harold Stott, who was round and rosy and carried a briefcase.
Mr Conrad Vane walked straight into the hall and pinned a white notice to the board. It said that the garden would soon be sold to a firm of builders, who planned to put new flats on it.
Gwen Hartley arrived at the board with her stick raised, as if she meant to fight the notice. She told everyone who would listen that she had planted every rose in the garden with her own two hands.
Mr Vane replied coldly that business was business, and that roses could surely be planted somewhere else. Gwen's face went white, and her stick tapped hard on the floor.
Joe Bell came up from the garden with soil on his hands and shouted that the sale would cost him his job. Mr Vane only looked at his watch and said that the builders would not need a gardener.
Edith did not join the shouting, because she preferred to watch. When Mr Vane looked down the garden toward the glasshouse, she thought she saw something like regret cross his face.

That afternoon the Wednesday Club met in a hurry and agreed to write a petition against the sale. Meera promised to knock on every door in the building, and Walter said that he would write to the council.
On Friday afternoon Mr Vane called every resident into the lounge and told them that the sale was final. Harold Stott stood beside him with his briefcase and smiled, as though it were good news.
On Saturday the garden was full of colour, because the summer fair had come round again. There were flags on the fence, a cake stall, a raffle and a brass band on the lawn.
Gwen had a stall of seedlings and cut roses, with a sign that said Save Our Garden. Joe Bell put up the tents and hammered every peg as if it were Mr Vane's hat.
At the cake stall Walter waved a leaflet and complained that the railway was closed for repairs all weekend. Buses were running instead of trains, he said, and he thought it was a disgrace.
Mr Vane walked slowly round the fair with his hands in his pockets, and nobody spoke to him. At Gwen's stall he stopped and looked for a long time at a single pink rose.

Gwen told him that the rose was the oldest in the garden, and then, quite suddenly, she pushed a crumpled paper into his hand. It was a letter from her bank about her care fees, which she had never understood, and Mr Vane frowned as he read it.
Later that afternoon Meera went down to buy a tomato plant and saw Mr Vane through the glass of the glasshouse. He was sitting alone at the potting bench, writing slowly on a sheet of paper.
Mr Vane stopped at the cake stall and told Lucy Pym that he had a meeting at nine o'clock that night. It would be in the glasshouse, he said, and nobody was to disturb him.

Harold Stott strolled across the lawn with a long fawn raincoat over his arm, although the sky was perfectly blue. When Edith remarked on it, he laughed and said that he never trusted an English summer.

Over a cup of tea in the tent, Stott told Edith that he must leave at six o'clock to catch the six-fifteen train to London. He had a quiet weekend at home ahead of him, he said, and a great deal of paperwork.

At exactly six o'clock Harold Stott signed out in the visitors' book at the front desk, with a great flourish of his brass pen. Then he picked up his briefcase, put his raincoat over his arm and walked out of the front door.

When the last stall had been packed away, Joe put his tools in the shed and washed his hands. He was spending the night at his daughter Pat's house, and he set off down the lane with his cap in his pocket.
At seven o'clock Lucy served supper in the dining room, and the residents ate well after the long day. Mr Vane did not appear, so she covered his plate and left it on a tray in the hall.
After supper the four friends sat together in the Garden Room while the evening grew soft and gold. They talked about the strange Mr Vane, who had been cold in the morning and sad in the afternoon.
At nine o'clock Gwen remembered that she had left her unsold seedlings on a bench near the glasshouse. She took her stick and a small torch and went out into the dusk to fetch them.
As Gwen came near the glasshouse, she saw that a light was burning inside it. A man in a long raincoat stood with his back to her, and his collar was turned up.
Gwen did not want to disturb a meeting that was none of her business, so she left the seedlings where they were. She walked back along the path, locked her door and went to bed with a mild headache.
The night passed quietly over Maple Court, and the clock in the church tower chimed every hour. At the end of the garden the lamp in the glasshouse burned on until morning, and nobody saw it.
On Sunday morning Joe Bell came back early from his daughter's house, because the tomatoes needed watering. The sun was only just up, and the dew was still thick on the grass.

The glasshouse door was locked, as it should have been, so Joe took out his own key and turned it in the lock. Inside the warm green air, Mr Vane lay on the floor between the benches, and he did not move.
Joe ran across the lawn faster than he had run in thirty years. He hammered on the office door, shouted for help and rang the police with shaking fingers.
A police car arrived within twenty minutes, and a tall young man in uniform climbed out of it. He introduced himself as Sergeant Tom Rudd and asked Joe to tell him slowly everything he had seen.
The doctor came soon afterwards, a tired man who had been called away from his Sunday breakfast. He knelt beside Mr Vane for a few minutes while the sergeant walked slowly around the glasshouse.
After a short talk the two men agreed that Mr Vane had slipped on the wet floor and hit his head. The sergeant telephoned his inspector, and by ten o'clock the matter was closed as an accident.
The sergeant spoke to the residents in the lounge, and many of them were still in their dressing gowns. He told them gently that Mr Vane had died in a fall, and that it was nobody's fault.

Later that morning a grey van drove slowly down the drive, and Meera held the front door open while the residents stood at their windows. Sergeant Rudd telephoned Mr Vane's sister, Ruth, who said that she would come as soon as she could.
In the afternoon Edith took her notebook and walked down the garden to the glasshouse. She stood outside the door for a long time, looking at the lock and at the lamp that had burned all night.
That evening the Wednesday Club met on a Sunday for the first time in its history. Nobody wanted cake, and the plate stayed empty while Edith put her notebook on the table.

Edith counted her worries on her fingers: no supper, a night alone in the glasshouse, and a lamp that burned until morning. A man who looked so troubled all day, she said, does not simply slip on a wet floor.

Walter agreed that the verdict had been remarkably quick, and he said that he knew a rushed timetable when he saw one. The inspector wanted his Sunday, he said, and a sad accident was the cheapest explanation to hand.

Edith asked whether the club was ready to do what it had never done before, and look into a real death. The answer came from all three at once, and Fergus said that he would begin with the lock in the morning.
On Monday morning the four friends walked down to the glasshouse, and Fergus knelt in front of the door. He took a small lens from his pocket and studied the lock for a very long time.
At last Fergus stood up and explained that the glasshouse door had a keyhole on the outside only. Inside there was just a plain handle, so nobody could lock the door from within.
Walter said slowly that a man who has fallen cannot turn a key behind himself. Somebody had stood outside and locked the door while Mr Vane lay on the floor.
Joe was weeding nearby, and he told them that only three keys fitted the glasshouse lock. One was Mr Vane's, one was his own, and the third was a spare kept in the office.

Joe took them to the estate office, where a grey steel cabinet hung on the wall beside the window. He tapped in the four-figure code with his back turned, and inside the cabinet the spare key hung quietly on its hook.

Back in the Garden Room Edith drew three keys in her notebook and wrote a question mark beside each. Whoever had locked the door had used one of them, she said, and had then put it back or carried it away.
Meera at last told the others what she had seen when the sheet slipped on the stretcher. Mr Vane had a dark mark at the back of his head, and she was sure it was not an ordinary bruise.
Joe had said that Mr Vane was lying on his front, Meera pointed out. A man who falls forward bruises his hands, his knees and his forehead, but he does not hit the back of his head.
That afternoon Edith found Sergeant Rudd on the front steps and told him about the lock and about Meera's wound. She asked him politely, in her headteacher's voice, to keep the case open.
Rudd glanced around and whispered that a shelf of red clay pots had been pulled down on top of Mr Vane. Nobody else knew, he said, and she must promise to tell no one, not even her friends.
On Tuesday the friends found Joe in his potting shed, sitting with a mug of tea and a worried frown. He admitted straight away that he had quarrelled with Mr Vane, and he said he knew how it looked.
Joe told them that he had spent Saturday night at his daughter Pat's house on the other side of town. Her son Sam, who was ten, had beaten him at cards until midnight.
Joe said that he would never harm a living thing in that garden, and his hands closed gently around a rose cutting. Edith watched his face and could find nothing false in it.
Joe said that his glasshouse key had never left the chain on his belt, even at his daughter's house. Mr Vane had told him at the fair that he would look after the glasshouse himself that evening.

In her flowered armchair Gwen listened to the friends' questions and then announced that she had seen something on Saturday night. At nine o'clock she had walked down to fetch her seedlings, and she had seen a light in the glasshouse.
Gwen could not describe his face, because he had stood with his back to her the whole time. All she remembered was a long raincoat, a turned-up collar and the way he stood so very still.
Edith wrote the word raincoat in her notebook and underlined it twice. Nobody wore a raincoat on a warm, dry night, she said, unless he wanted to hide his clothes or his face.
In the kitchen Lucy showed them the tray she had left for Mr Vane, which was still untouched. She said that he had told her at the fair about a meeting at nine o'clock in the glasshouse.
Lucy did not know whom Mr Vane had arranged to meet, because he had not said. He had seemed tired but strangely lighter, as if he had decided something that had been troubling him.

That night Edith wrote a new heading across a clean page of her notebook: whom had Mr Vane meant to meet at nine o'clock? Underneath it she wrote the names of everyone who had been at the fair and might have known.
Edith asked to see the visitors' book at the front desk and turned back to Saturday. Between the end of the fair and midnight, only one person had signed out, and that person was Harold Stott.

Stott's name was written with a splendid flourish, and beside it, in the same confident ink, he had noted the time as six o'clock exactly. Nobody else in the whole book ever bothered to write down the time.

On Tuesday afternoon the friends knocked on the door of Stott's office, which was as tidy as a new pin. The desk shone, the pens stood in a row, and a long fawn raincoat hung on a hook behind the door.

Stott told them in a soft, sad voice that he had left at six o'clock and caught the six-fifteen train to London. He had spent the whole of Sunday at home and had not heard the dreadful news until Monday morning.
When Fergus asked about the sale, Stott replied that Mr Vane's wishes were clear and that one had to be practical. The builders were waiting, and the garden would be sold exactly as planned.
Edith asked mildly what the journey had been like and who had sat beside him on the train. Stott answered every question at once, as if he had practised the answers in front of a mirror.

On the way out Fergus asked about the grey steel cabinet in the estate office next door and what was kept inside it. Stott said that it held spare keys and nothing more, and that he hardly ever touched it.

On the potting bench Edith noticed a small round tin among the neat, labelled boxes. Every other box had a name written on it in Joe's square handwriting, but the tin had none.

Walter read the letter over Edith's shoulder and whistled softly. The man who had pinned up the notice on Monday had changed his mind by Saturday, he said, and had died the same night.

Sergeant Rudd slid the letter into a clear plastic bag and promised to lock it in his safe. Edith asked the question that had been growing in her mind: who else knew that Mr Vane had changed his mind?

Edith stood apart from the crowd, tapping her pencil against her lip and thinking hard. Stott would hardly have posted this notice if he had known about the letter, so either he did not know or he was very clever.
That afternoon a small grey car arrived, and a tired woman in a dark coat stepped out. She was Ruth Vane, Conrad's sister, and she had driven for six hours without a proper meal.

Soon afterwards a heavy man with rolled plans under his arm strode into the hall and demanded to see Mr Stott. He was Dennis Kemp of Kemp and Sons, the builders who were waiting to buy the garden.
Fergus overheard Kemp complaining that his money had been ready since Monday and that he had been promised the garden. Stott soothed him in a low voice and said that Mr Vane's death changed nothing.
That evening Edith added two more names to her list. Dennis Kemp would lose a great deal if the sale failed, and Ruth Vane, as the only relative, would inherit Maple Court.
Edith drew a table with three columns: who wanted the sale, who wanted to stop it, and who could reach a key. The names crossed over in surprising places, and she frowned at it for an hour.

At the next meeting Edith asked whether they wanted to go on, since the work was proving harder than any newspaper puzzle. Every hand went up before she had finished the question, and Lucy brought in the lemon cake.
Gwen's eyes were tired, so she asked Meera to help her with a bank statement that had arrived that morning. They sat together under the reading lamp with a pot of tea between them.
Meera ran her finger down the page and stopped. The care fee appeared twice each month, once under its proper name and once under a slightly different one that was easy to miss.

Meera and Fergus went from door to door along the corridor with a notebook and a plate of cake. They asked the residents very politely whether they could look at their monthly statements.

Ravi Anand, the retired bus conductor, was the first to open his door, and Tilly Drummond, who was knitting, was the second. Their statements showed the same two lines in each month, one proper and one extra.
By the end of the afternoon they had seen eleven statements, and every one of them showed the extra fee. Each resident had been paying the same fee twice, and nobody had noticed.

Meera looked back through the older statements and saw that the extra fee had started about a year ago. It began when the new company took over the accounts, and before that every resident had paid the right amount.
Meera brought the figures to Edith, who listened without a word. Somebody had been taking money from the residents, she said, and the person who looked after the billing was the finance manager.
Gwen reminded them that Mr Vane had read her crumpled paper at the fair and had gone very quiet. He had folded it into his pocket, she said, and she had not seen it since.
Edith wrote two words on a clean page and underlined them: Vane knew. If Mr Vane had understood the extra fees on Saturday, she thought, then somebody had a very good reason to keep him quiet.
A few mornings later Edith watched Harold Stott cross the hall in his gleaming black shoes. In the light from the window she saw a thin line of red dust along the edge of one sole.

That afternoon Edith walked every path of the garden with her eyes on the ground. There was grey gravel and green lawn and brown earth, but there was no red dust anywhere except inside the glasshouse.

Mr Greaves showed Walter the replacement timetable for the weekend of the repairs. The only bus to the city that evening left at twenty past six, and the next one did not go until eleven.

Walter found the driver of the six-twenty bus, a cheerful woman called Nina Doyle, drinking tea beside her bus. She had carried only six passengers that night, she said, and none of them had been a round man in a good suit.

That evening Walter laid his bus ticket on the table in the Garden Room and told the others what he had found. Edith said quietly that Stott had lied about the train, and that the best reason for such a lie was that he had not left.
Fergus asked Joe whether he might look again at the cabinet and the spare key. Joe opened it with his back turned, and Sergeant Rudd, who happened to be passing, said that he would allow it.

Fergus lifted the spare key by its paper tag and tilted it toward the window. In the folds of the paper and in the ring of the key there was a trace of fine red dust.

They asked Lucy who knew the code, and she answered at once, because she wished to be helpful. Only three people knew it, she said: Joe, Mr Stott and herself.
Lucy swore that she had not taken the key. She had served supper until half past eight, she said, and had then sat in the lounge with the residents until ten o'clock.

Edith crossed Lucy and Joe off her list for the night in question. That left only Harold Stott, who had known the code, and who had said that he was on a train.
Fergus walked the length of the garden and found a green gate hidden behind a rose bush. It opened from the lane with a simple latch, so a man could return without passing the front door.

Edith stood at the green gate and looked up the dusky garden toward the glasshouse. A man could have slipped in unseen, she said, but a possibility is not proof, and proof was what the sergeant would need.

The sergeant thought it over carefully and then shook his head. Stott could say he had visited the glasshouse earlier that week, he said, and a bus driver might easily forget a face.

Edith said nothing, but she was thinking of the secret that the sergeant had told her on the steps. Only the killer, the sergeant, the doctor and Joe knew about the shelf of pots.

Edith proposed a residents' meeting for the Thursday of the following week, at which Stott would be asked to speak about the sale. She herself would speak afterwards and tell the sad news very carefully.
Edith drew a plan in her notebook with four small circles for the friends and one large cross for Stott. Every circle had a job to do, and each job was written in her tidiest handwriting.

Rudd agreed to wait in the next room with the door open a crack, ready to step in at a word from Edith. Joe, who was asked to stand at the back of the lounge, would say nothing unless somebody spoke his name.
That night Edith sat at her window with a cup of mint tea, looking at the dark shape of the glasshouse. She had never been so nervous before a lesson, and she had taught a great many lessons.
On Wednesday afternoon the friends set out chairs in the Garden Room exactly as they would stand in the lounge. Meera moved from seat to seat to play the whole crowd of residents.
Walter practised his part about the train, but he began with the invention of the steam engine. Edith took his card, drew a firm line through most of it and handed it back.
Meera practised holding up the statements and explaining the double fees in a quiet voice. Her hands shook at first, so Fergus lent her a clipboard to hold.

Fergus practised holding up a stand-in key and saying his lines, and on the first attempt the key slid out of his fingers. It struck the floor with a clatter, and for the first time in three weeks the whole club laughed.
Gwen heard about the plan and insisted on a seat in the front row. She said that she would tap her stick whenever she heard a lie, and Edith begged her to do nothing of the kind.

Lucy had been told only that there would be an important meeting, and she baked a lemon cake for it without being asked. Nobody was ever brave on an empty stomach, she said, and she was probably right.
Edith told Ruth Vane just enough of the plan to win her trust. Ruth agreed to sit in the front row beside Gwen, and she promised to keep her face still whatever she heard.
Joe grumbled that he was a gardener and not an actor, but he agreed to stand at the back with his arms folded. He would say nothing, he promised, unless Edith asked him a question.

On Wednesday evening Edith left her notebook on a hall table for a moment, and Harold Stott picked it up with a polite smile. She took it back from him at once and told him sweetly that it was only her shopping list.
On the night before the meeting Edith walked down to the glasshouse in the moonlight and stood at its door. The tomatoes inside were ripening in the dark, and she felt strangely calm.
On Thursday morning the lounge slowly filled with residents, who carried their own cushions and cups of tea. By ten o'clock every chair was taken, and Lucy's lemon cake stood ready on a long table.
Harold Stott arrived at five past ten, smiling broadly and carrying his briefcase. His shoes shone brighter than ever, and he took his place at the front as though he owned the room.
Sergeant Rudd had slipped into the little sitting room next door before anyone arrived. He had left the door open exactly the width of a notebook, and he sat very straight on a hard chair.
Stott rose, spread his hands and spoke to the residents in his warm, smooth voice. He was very sorry, he said, but the sale of the garden must go ahead, and the builders would arrive in the autumn.
A long groan went around the room, and somebody at the back called out that it was a shame. Gwen held her stick tightly in both hands and did not tap it, though it clearly cost her a great deal.
Edith rose from her seat and asked, very politely, whether she might say a few words. Stott waved a gracious hand and said that of course she might, since she was the wisest member of the house.

Edith spoke quietly and simply to the room, reminding everyone that Mr Vane had been found dead in the glasshouse. The police had called it a fall, she said, but nobody had explained why he was there so late.
Stott shook his head and sighed heavily, as if the whole matter were too painful to bear. Poor Mr Vane, he said, lying there under all those pots that somebody had pulled down on top of him.

There was a silence in the lounge so complete that people could hear the clock on the mantelpiece. Then Gwen, who had promised to tap just once, brought her stick down on the floor with a single clear crack.
Edith asked him quietly how he knew that the pots had been pulled down. Nobody at Maple Court had been told that, she said, and she had certainly not mentioned it.
Stott went pale, and his smile slid sideways like a picture hung crooked. He said, rather too quickly, that somebody must have told him, and that he rather thought it was Joe.
Joe unfolded his arms at the back of the room and said in his gruff voice that he had told no one. He had spoken of it only to the sergeant, and he had done so in the glasshouse with the door shut.
Stott tried again and said that perhaps it was Lucy who had told him. Lucy, who was standing at the door with a tea tray, said in a small clear voice that she had never even seen the pots.

Walter stood up with a yellow railway notice in both hands and said that he had a question about the six-fifteen train. There had not been one on that Saturday, he said, because the line was closed for repairs.
Stott swallowed and said that of course he had taken the replacement bus, and that he had used the word train from habit. It was an easy mistake, he said, and anyone could have made it.
Walter said calmly that the only replacement bus had left at twenty past six, and that its driver remembered all six of her passengers. None of them had been a round, rosy man in a good suit.

Meera rose with her clipboard and said that eleven residents had been charged their care fee twice every month for a year. She asked Mr Stott, as the manager of the accounts, whether he could explain it.
Stott replied hurriedly that it was merely an accounting error and that he would put it right at once. His voice had risen, though, and a muscle was twitching in his cheek.
Fergus stood and held up the spare glasshouse key, whose tag still carried the red dust. Only three people had known the code of the cabinet, he said, and Mr Stott was one of them.
Harold Stott looked around the room at the faces of the people he had robbed. Not one of them was smiling, and his great round face slowly turned the colour of paper.
Harold Stott's knees gave way, and he sank into the nearest chair with his head in his hands. The room waited, and nobody offered him a handkerchief.
He said that he had taken the money, a little at a time, over the whole of the last year. He had borrowed more than he could repay, and he had told himself that nobody would ever miss it.

Mr Vane had seen Gwen's bank paper at the fair, Stott said, and he had understood the scheme in a minute. That afternoon he had called Stott aside and told him to bring the account books to the glasshouse at nine o'clock.

He had signed out at six o'clock on purpose, he said, so that everyone would think he had gone. Then he had parked his silver car behind the church and waited for the dark, with his raincoat buttoned over his good suit.
When it was nearly dark he had come back through the green gate at the bottom of the garden. He had slipped into the estate office, tapped in the code and taken the spare key from its hook.

Mr Vane had been waiting at the potting bench, Stott said, with a pile of account books and a tired, steady face. He had said that the sale was cancelled, that every pound must be repaid, and that the police would be told on Monday.
In a moment of terrible panic, Stott said, he had picked up a heavy clay pot and struck Mr Vane once from behind. Mr Vane had fallen without a sound, and he had not moved again.
Then, Stott said, he had pulled a whole shelf of red pots down over Mr Vane so that it would look like a dreadful accident. He had thought it very clever at the time.

He had pushed the spare key into the lock with trembling fingers, Stott said, and he had scratched the brass in his hurry. Then he had returned it to the cabinet and left the lamp burning, because he had forgotten all about it.
When he had finished, nobody in the lounge said a word. Edith had expected to feel proud of herself, but she felt only a heavy sadness for Conrad Vane, who had changed his mind too late.

Sergeant Rudd stepped through the door of the next room, where he had heard every word. He took Stott gently by the arm and told him that he was under arrest for the death of Conrad Vane and for stealing money.
Stott was led out through the hall, and his polished shoes clicked on the floor. The residents stood in silence on either side, and nobody said a word until the front door had closed.
Sergeant Rudd shook Edith's hand and thanked the whole club with an unsteady smile. Inspector Hale, he said, would be changing his mind that very afternoon, and would not enjoy it.
The police searched Stott's tidy office and his silver car. In the boot they found the missing account books, and behind the office door hung a long fawn raincoat with red dust on its sleeves.

Over the following weeks the police followed the stolen money through four bank accounts, and most of it was found. Ruth Vane made up the rest from her brother's money, saying that it was what Conrad would have wanted.
One bright morning eleven residents opened identical envelopes and found their money back, to the last penny. Ravi Anand laughed out loud, and Gwen cried happily into her teacup.
Ruth Vane now owned Maple Court, as her brother's only family, and Sergeant Rudd brought her Conrad's letter from the police safe. She read it three times, standing very still by the window.
Ruth signed a legal paper that said the garden of Maple Court would never be sold. Dennis Kemp read it with a sour face, rolled up his plans and drove away to find another field.
Ruth told Joe that he would be the head gardener of Maple Court for as long as he wanted the job. She gave him a new wheelbarrow with a blue bow on it, and Joe nearly smiled.
Gwen chose a pink rose, the colour that Conrad Vane had loved, and planted it beside the glasshouse. Joe dug the hole, and Ruth poured the first can of water.
On the following Sunday the residents gathered by the glasshouse in their best clothes to remember Conrad Vane. Nobody had known him well, but everybody had come to understand him a little.
Ruth asked Joe to show her how to plant the tomato seeds from the old seed tin. The glasshouse smelled of fresh earth and water again, and it began to feel like a happy place.
In the Garden Room the four friends sat among the cushions and talked about what they had done. They had solved a real case, said Fergus, and not one of them could quite believe it.
That evening Edith opened a fresh notebook and wrote the date at the top of a clean page. She had never expected to need another one, and she was surprised by how much she hoped to.

At the next meeting Lucy carried in a lemon cake with a single candle burning in the middle of it. She said that it was a thank-you to the Wednesday Club, and she blew her nose loudly before anyone could comment.

A week later Sergeant Rudd appeared at the Garden Room door, carrying a box of cakes and a thick folder. He cleared his throat and asked, rather shyly, whether the club might help him with another puzzle.
Rudd opened the folder on the table, and four heads leaned over it at once. Inside was a puzzle from Willowby itself: a rare old book that had vanished from the town library twenty years ago.

Walter said that he would check every date in the library records, and Fergus said that he wanted to see the locks. Meera promised to talk to the old librarians, and Edith opened a new page in her notebook.

As the afternoon turned to evening, the four friends carried their tea out into the garden and sat among the roses. The new pink rose stood beside the glasshouse, and it already looked as if it belonged.

In the long gold light the four friends sat among the roses with their tea, and the glasshouse glowed behind them like a lantern. The trouble was over, the garden was safe, and the next puzzle was waiting in a folder on Edith's knee.

Its residents were fond of it in the way that one is fond of an old and difficult friend.

Behind the house ran a long garden, with a rose walk on one side, a vegetable patch on the other and, at the far end, a glasshouse that shone in the afternoon sun. Joe Bell had looked after the garden for twenty years, a gruff and weathered man who spoke little and grumbled often about the weather. He knew every plant in the garden by name and every slug in it by reputation. If a rose bush was unwell, he could tell from the far end of the path.

Gwen Hartley, who was eighty-eight and walked with a stick, had planted every rose along the path with her own hands. She talked to them every morning, and she claimed, with a perfectly straight face, that they answered back. Nobody at Maple Court had the heart or the courage to argue with her about it.

Lucy Pym, the young cook, had come to Maple Court two years earlier with a battered recipe book and a real gift for baking. Her lemon cake was so light and so sharp that the residents forgave her anything, even the occasional burnt toast. She was always in a hurry, and she was always humming a tune as she went.

Every Wednesday at three o'clock, four friends settled into the armchairs of the Garden Room, a bright and slightly shabby room that looked out over the lawn. She was calm and sharp, and she kept a small notebook in her cardigan pocket, where she wrote down anything that failed to add up. The others secretly agreed that she was the leader of the club, although she never said so.

Walter Pike had spent forty years in a railway signal box, watching the trains of three counties come and go like beads on a string. He still carried the timetables in his head, and he took any delay or change as a personal insult. The others had learned never to ask him the time unless they had an hour to spare.

Meera Shah had nursed the sick for forty years, and she had learned that a calm voice could settle almost any storm. She noticed small things about people, such as a pale cheek or an unsteady hand, long before they noticed them for themselves. In the club she was the one who asked the quiet question that nobody else had thought to ask.

Fergus Lyle had picked, mended and made locks for fifty years, and his gnarled hands still moved with a delicate certainty that surprised strangers. He believed that every lock had a character of its own, and that a good one should be admired like a fine violin. Together with Edith, Walter and Meera, he made up the most unlikely company of detectives to be found anywhere in the county.

Nobody at all expected the afternoon to be anything other than pleasant and rather slow.

Fergus proved that the hotel safe could never have been opened without its key, while Walter pointed out, with great satisfaction, that the thief's famous midnight train had not run on that night at all. Gwen Hartley reached the board just as the last pin went in, and she raised her walking stick like a knight with a lance. Edith nodded and drank her tea, and she tucked the time away in her memory, as she tucked away everything.

At exactly six o'clock Harold Stott signed out in the visitors' book at the front desk, with a great flourish of his brass pen and a nod to the empty hall.
