The fair was packing up behind him, and nobody thought of him again that night.

When the last stall had been packed away, Joe Bell put his tools in the shed, washed the soil from his hands and took his cap from its nail. He was spending the night at his daughter Pat's house on the far side of Willowby, as he always did on the night of the fair, and he set off down the lane at a steady walk. As he passed the glasshouse, he saw Mr Vane inside, bending over the potting bench in the glow of a small lamp, and he said nothing at all.

At seven o'clock Lucy served supper in the dining room, and the residents ate like people who had earned it after a long and noisy day. Mr Vane did not appear, so she covered a plate with a silver lid and left it on a tray in the hall in case he should want it later. Hours afterwards, when everything had changed, it would still be sitting there, quite untouched and growing cold.

After supper the four friends sat together in the Garden Room while the evening turned soft and gold outside the windows. They talked about the strange Mr Vane, who had been so cold on Monday and who had stood all afternoon at the fair like a man arguing with himself. Edith said little, but her pencil moved in her notebook, and nobody dared to ask what she was writing.

At nine o'clock Gwen suddenly remembered that she had left her unsold seedlings on a bench near the glasshouse, and she could not bear the thought of them spending the night alone. She took her stick and a small torch and set off down the garden path as the last of the daylight faded. The air smelled of cut grass and warm roses, and she hummed to herself as she went.

As she drew near the glasshouse, Gwen saw that a lamp was burning inside it and that its glass walls glowed like a ship on the dark lawn. A man in a long raincoat stood with his back to her among the benches, and his collar was turned up as if against a wind that was not blowing. She could not see his face, and she was far too polite to stare.

Gwen had no wish to interrupt a meeting that was plainly none of her business, so she left her seedlings where they stood and tiptoed back along the path. She locked her door, drank a cup of warm milk and went to bed with the comfortable feeling of a day well spent. It never occurred to her that what she had seen would matter to anybody.

The night passed quietly over Maple Court, and the clock in the church tower chimed each hour to a sleeping town. At the far end of the garden the glasshouse lamp burned on alone until dawn, because the windows of the old house looked the other way and nobody was awake to wonder at it. A fox crossed the lawn at three o'clock and paused to stare at the glowing glass.

On Sunday morning Joe Bell walked back from his daughter's house before the sun had properly risen, because the tomatoes in the glasshouse would not water themselves. The dew lay thick on the grass, a blackbird was singing on the shed roof, and he felt almost cheerful until he reached the end of the path. The lamp was still burning there, pale and rather foolish in the daylight, and that was the first thing that troubled him.

The glasshouse door was locked, as it should have been at that hour, so Joe took out his own key and turned it in the lock. Inside the warm green air, Mr Vane lay motionless on the floor between the benches, one arm stretched out as if he had been reaching for something. Joe knew at once, with the certainty of a man who had seen a great deal of life, that nothing could be done.

Joe ran across the dew-soaked lawn faster than he had run in thirty years, his cap lost somewhere behind him in the grass. He hammered on the door of the office, shouted until the first lights came on in the upstairs windows and telephoned the police with hands that would not stop shaking. Within minutes the peaceful Sunday morning at Maple Court had turned into something very different indeed.

A police car arrived within twenty minutes, and a tall young man in uniform unfolded himself from the driving seat with an air of careful politeness. He introduced himself as Sergeant Tom Rudd, took out a notebook that looked brand new and asked Joe to tell him slowly, and in order, everything he had seen. Joe obeyed, twisting his hands, and by the end of it the sergeant had filled three whole pages.

The doctor arrived soon afterwards, a tired and rumpled man who had plainly been called away from his Sunday breakfast. He knelt beside Mr Vane for only a few minutes, murmuring to himself, while the sergeant walked slowly around the glasshouse and studied everything with his hands behind his back. Joe stood at the door with his hands hanging uselessly at his sides and his eyes on the floor.

After a short and murmured conversation, the two men agreed that Mr Vane had slipped on the wet floor, struck his head and died where he fell. The sergeant telephoned his inspector, a busy man named Hale who disliked working on Sundays, and by ten o'clock the matter had been closed as a sad accident. Nobody stopped to ask a single awkward question, and nobody seemed to want to.

The sergeant spoke to the residents in the lounge, where many of them were still in their dressing gowns and holding cups of tea that they had forgotten to drink. He told them gently that Mr Vane had died after a fall in the glasshouse and that it had been an accident, which was nobody's fault. A long hush followed, and then somebody began to cry quietly in the corner.

Later that morning a grey van drove slowly down the drive between the rose beds, and Meera held the front door open while the residents stood at their windows in respectful silence. Sergeant Rudd telephoned Mr Vane's only relative, his sister Ruth, who said in a small flat voice that she would come as soon as she could. Lucy sat down on a kitchen stool and cried into a dish towel, though she had hardly known the man.

In the afternoon, when the garden had grown quiet again, Edith took her notebook and walked down the path to the glasshouse by herself. She stood outside the door for a long time, looking at the lock, at the dark glass and at the small lamp that had burned all night without anyone asking why. Something about the morning's quick verdict sat in her mind like a stone in a shoe.

That evening the Wednesday Club met on a Sunday for the first time in its history, and the mood in the Garden Room was unlike anything it had known. Nobody wanted cake, the teapot grew cold, and an empty plate sat in the middle of the table like a small white moon. Edith laid her notebook down in front of her and said that she did not believe a word of the accident.

Edith counted her worries on her fingers: Mr Vane had missed his supper, he had been alone in the glasshouse long after dark, and the lamp had burned there until morning. She reminded them that a man who had looked so troubled all day does not simply slip on a wet floor, and that nobody had troubled to ask why he was there. Her three friends looked at one another across the cold teapot, and none of them argued.

Walter agreed that the verdict had been remarkably quick, and he remarked that he had seen a great many rushed timetables in his time and none of them had ever ended well. The inspector wanted his Sunday, he said, and a sad accident was the cheapest explanation to hand. Meera added quietly that she had noticed something as the stretcher passed, and that she wanted to think about it before she spoke.

Edith asked whether the club was prepared to do something it had never done in all its years of cheerful guessing, and look into a real death. The answer came from all three of them at once, and it was yes, and Fergus added that he would begin in the morning with the lock on the glasshouse door. Outside the window the garden lay silent in the dusk, and the glasshouse stood at the end of it like a question that nobody had yet answered.

On Monday morning the four friends walked down the garden to the glasshouse, and Fergus lowered himself stiffly onto his knees in front of the door. He took a small brass lens from his waistcoat pocket and studied the lock for a long and silent minute, as a doctor studies a patient. Walter, who was not a patient man, shifted from foot to foot until Edith frowned at him.

At last Fergus rose, brushed off his knees and explained that the glasshouse door had a keyhole on the outside and nothing but a plain handle on the inside. It was an old and honest lock, he said, with a good heavy bolt, and it could be turned only by somebody who stood on the garden side with a key in his hand. Nobody could possibly lock himself inside that glasshouse, he said, even if he tried for a week.

Walter said slowly that a man who has fallen and died cannot turn a key behind himself, and that the sergeant had simply overlooked the fact. Somebody had stood on the garden side of that door, turned the key and walked away with Mr Vane lying inside. The four friends were silent, and a thrush went on singing on the roof as though nothing in the world had changed.

Joe was weeding nearby, and he told them gruffly that only three keys fitted the glasshouse lock. One had belonged to Mr Vane, one hung on the chain at Joe's own belt, and the third was a spare kept in the office. The sergeant, he added with a sniff, had found Mr Vane's key in the dead man's jacket pocket.

Joe took them to the estate office, where a grey steel cabinet hung on the wall beside the window, and he tapped in its four-figure code with his broad back turned politely toward them. Inside, the spare glasshouse key hung on a small brass hook, exactly where it was supposed to be. Fergus, who had a locksmith's reverence for any good steel box, nodded in approval and said that it was a better cabinet than the house deserved.

Back in the Garden Room Edith drew three keys in her notebook and wrote a question mark beside each of them. Whoever had locked that door had used one of the three, she said, and had afterwards either put it back in its place or carried it away. It was the first real clue the club had ever held, and it felt oddly heavy in the hand.

Meera at last told the others what she had glimpsed when the sheet slipped on the stretcher. Mr Vane had a dark and swollen mark at the very back of his head, and she was quite sure that it was not an ordinary bruise from a fall. Her voice was steady, but her hands were folded so tightly in her lap that the knuckles showed white.

Joe had told them that Mr Vane was lying on his face, Meera pointed out, and she had seen a great many falls in forty years of nursing. A man who falls forward grazes his hands and knees and perhaps his forehead, but he does not strike the back of his head, and certainly not so hard. Somebody else, she concluded in her calm voice, must have been standing behind him.

That afternoon Edith found Sergeant Rudd on the front steps and laid out the lock, the three keys and Meera's wound as neatly as a teacher laying out a lesson plan. She asked him, politely and in a voice that had never failed in thirty years, to keep the case open for a little longer. The young sergeant looked at his shoes, then at the garden and then, at last, at her.

Rudd glanced over both shoulders and told her in a low voice that a whole shelf of heavy red clay pots had been pulled down on top of Mr Vane, a detail that the inspector had preferred to forget. Only he, the doctor and Joe knew it, he said, and he begged her to tell no one, not even her three friends. Edith gave her word, and she kept it, which was harder than she had expected.

On Tuesday the friends found Joe in his potting shed, hunched on an upturned crate with a mug of tea going cold between his hands. He admitted at once that he had quarrelled bitterly with Mr Vane, and he said that he knew perfectly well how that would look to the police. His honesty was so plain and so awkward that Edith found herself liking him immediately, and she hoped it would not cloud her judgment.

Joe told them that he had spent the whole of Saturday night at his daughter Pat's house on the far side of Willowby, where he always slept after the fair. Her son Sam, who was ten and ruthless, had beaten him at cards until midnight, and Pat herself had made up a bed for him on the sofa. Pat would say so to anyone who asked, he added, and so would the boy, who was still annoyed about the cards.

Joe said that he had never harmed a living thing in that garden in twenty years, and his rough hands closed gently around a rose cutting as he spoke. He had shouted at Mr Vane, he admitted, because he was frightened for his work and for the roses, and he was sorry now that their last words had been angry ones. Edith watched his face closely and could find nothing false in it anywhere, not even in the corners of his eyes.

Joe tapped the heavy ring of keys on his belt and said that the glasshouse key had never left it, not even for a minute, and that it had spent Saturday night on the kitchen table at his daughter's house. Mr Vane, he went on, had told him at the fair in a curt voice that he would see to the glasshouse himself that evening. Joe had thought it rude at the time, but now he thought it simply sad.

In her flowered armchair Gwen listened to the friends' questions with her head on one side like a bird, and then she announced that she had seen something on Saturday night that she had told nobody. At nine o'clock she had walked down to fetch her seedlings, and she had seen a light burning in the glasshouse and a man standing inside it. She had not mentioned it before, she said, because nobody had asked her and because she did not like to gossip.

Gwen could not describe his face, because he had stood with his back to her the whole time and had never once turned round. All she could remember was a long raincoat, a collar turned up around the ears and the curious way he stood, very straight and very still, like someone waiting for an answer. She was certain of only one thing, which was that he had not been Mr Vane, because Mr Vane would have worn a suit.

Edith wrote the word raincoat in her notebook and underlined it twice with a firm pencil. Nobody put on a long raincoat with the collar turned up on a warm and perfectly dry night, she observed, unless he wished to hide his clothes or his face. Meera pointed out that it might mean nothing at all, and Edith agreed that it might, but she did not cross out the word.

In the kitchen Lucy showed the friends the tray she had left in the hall for Mr Vane on Saturday evening, which still held its silver lid and its cold dinner. Her eyes filled with tears as she explained that he had told her at the fair about a meeting at nine o'clock in the glasshouse. She had thought it strange at the time, she said, and she had thought about nothing else since.

Lucy twisted a dish towel in her hands and said that she did not know whom Mr Vane had arranged to meet, because he had not said. He had seemed tired, she remembered, but strangely lighter than before, like a man who has finally decided something that has been troubling him for a long time. She had liked him better on Saturday than on Monday, and she felt guilty about it now.

That night Edith wrote a new heading across a clean page of her notebook, and the heading was a question: whom had Mr Vane meant to meet at nine o'clock? Beneath it she wrote the names of everyone who had been at the fair, and she crossed out nobody, because as yet she had no reason to. The light in her window burned late, and across the dark garden the glasshouse stood silent and shut.

Edith asked to see the visitors' book that lay on the front desk, and she turned back the pages to Saturday with a careful finger. Between the end of the fair and midnight only one person had signed out, and that person was Harold Stott. Everybody else had come and gone through the garden gate, where nobody kept a book.

Stott's name was written with a splendid flourish, and beside it, in the same confident ink, he had noted the time: six o'clock exactly. Nobody else in the whole book ever bothered to write the time, Edith observed, and a man who makes sure that everyone knows when he left is sometimes a man who wishes to be believed. She did not say this aloud, but she copied the line into her notebook in her best handwriting.

On Tuesday afternoon the friends knocked on the door of Stott's office, which was as tidy as a new pin and smelled faintly of polish and coffee. The desk shone, the pens stood in a neat row like soldiers, and a long fawn raincoat hung innocently from the hook behind the door. Stott rose with a warm smile and offered them biscuits, as though they had come to collect a prize.

Stott folded his hands on the desk and told them, in a soft and sorrowful voice, that he had left Maple Court at six o'clock and caught the six-fifteen train to London. He had spent the whole of Sunday quietly at home, he said, and had not heard the dreadful news about Mr Vane until Monday morning. He dabbed one eye with a handkerchief, and Meera, who had seen real grief many times, noticed that the handkerchief stayed dry.

When Fergus asked about the sale, Stott replied smoothly that Mr Vane's wishes had been perfectly clear and that, in times of sorrow, one had to be practical. The builders were waiting, the papers were signed, and the garden would be sold exactly as planned, he said, with a little sigh that suggested it pained him deeply. Edith noticed that the sigh arrived a moment after the words, like an actor who has missed his cue.

Edith asked mildly what the journey had been like and who had sat beside him on the train. Stott answered at once that it had been crowded and dull and that he had stood all the way, with the speed of a man who has rehearsed his lines. Edith smiled sweetly, thanked him for the biscuit and wrote nothing down while he could see her, which in her was always a sign of great interest.

On the way out Fergus paused to ask, with a locksmith's innocent curiosity, about the grey steel cabinet in the estate office next door and what was kept inside it. Stott said lightly that it held the spare keys and nothing more interesting than that, and that in fact he hardly ever touched it. Fergus thanked him gravely and reflected that a man who has nothing to do with a cabinet does not usually explain it so fluently.

Outside the office Walter stopped on the steps and scratched his head, with the look of a man who has lost something small in a very large room. There was something about the six-fifteen train that nagged at him like a stone in a shoe, though he could not for the life of him say what. Meera told him kindly that it would come to him when he stopped trying, and she was right.

The next day, over a bowl of soup, Walter dropped his spoon with a clatter and announced that there had not been a single train on Saturday. The railway had been closed for track repairs all weekend, he reminded them with rising excitement, and he had complained about it for an hour at the fair. The three others stared at him, and the soup grew cold while the full meaning of his words settled over the table.

Edith wrote Harold Stott's name in her notebook and drew a small question mark beside it, though she was careful to remind her friends that a man who gets a train wrong has only made a mistake. A mistake, she said firmly, was not proof, and she had not spent thirty years teaching children to be fair in order to stop being fair now. Still, she added, it would do no harm to find out exactly what Mr Stott had been doing on Saturday night.

On Wednesday afternoon Sergeant Rudd appeared at the Garden Room door with a key in his hand and an apologetic smile on his face. He had decided that four retired people with a notebook could do the case no harm, he said, provided that they touched nothing and stayed close together. Edith thanked him gravely and secretly wondered which of them he thought was most likely to touch something.

Inside the glasshouse the air was warm and heavy with the green smell of tomato leaves, and the afternoon sun fell through the dusty glass in long gold bars. Benches of seedlings ran down both sides of the narrow aisle, and a wooden potting bench stood at the far end beneath a small lamp on a bracket. It seemed such a peaceful and cheerful place that the thought of what had happened there was almost impossible to bear.

Fergus went straight back to the door and studied the lock again from the outside, his lens held close to the brass. Around the keyhole he found a ring of fresh, bright scratches, the kind that a key leaves when it is pushed in by a hurried hand in poor light. A man who locks his own glasshouse every night, he told the others, does not make marks like that.

Walter pointed out the shelves of bright red clay pots that stood along the side wall, each stack as straight as a column of soldiers. There was a wide gap in the top row, and in the corner beneath it stood a bucket of broken pieces that somebody had swept up in a hurry. Edith looked at the bucket and said nothing, because she knew exactly what it meant and had promised not to tell.

Joe appeared in the doorway, still wiping his hands on a cloth, and told them that the red clay pots never left the glasshouse, because he had bought them for the tomatoes and for nothing else. Everything else in the garden was grey stone or green plastic, he said, and the paths were all grey gravel, so red dust could come from only one place. Edith did not write that down in her notebook, but she remembered every word of it exactly.

On the potting bench, among the neat rows of labelled boxes, Edith noticed a small round tin that did not belong there. Every other container on the bench carried a name written in Joe's square handwriting, but this one had been put down carelessly, with its lid slightly crooked. She asked the sergeant very politely whether she might look inside, and he nodded after only a moment of hesitation.

Edith lifted the lid with the tip of one finger and found a dozen packets of tomato seed, which gave off the faint dry smell of summer. Beneath them, folded into a small square, lay a sheet of good writing paper covered in a neat and slanting hand. The whole glasshouse seemed to hold its breath while she slowly and carefully unfolded the paper.

The letter was dated Saturday and signed Conrad Vane, and it was short and perfectly clear. He wrote that after a day among the roses and the residents he had changed his mind, that the sale was withdrawn and that the garden of Maple Court must never be sold to anyone at any price. At the bottom, under his signature, he had added a small line saying that he had been wrong to think that money was the only thing worth owning.

Walter read the letter over Edith's shoulder, and then he let out a long and rather shaky low whistle. The man who had pinned up the cold white notice on Monday had changed his mind by Saturday afternoon, he said slowly, and had been found dead by Sunday morning. Meera added that it was either the saddest coincidence in the history of Willowby or something very much worse.

Sergeant Rudd slid the letter into a clear plastic bag, wrote the date on it and promised to lock it in the police safe that very evening. Edith asked the question that had been growing in her mind ever since she had unfolded the paper, which was who else had known that Mr Vane had changed his mind. Nobody could answer it, and the four friends walked back up the garden in a thoughtful silence.

The next morning Harold Stott pinned a new notice to the board in the hall, using the same four brass pins that Mr Vane had used. It stated that, in spite of the sad death of Mr Vane, the sale of the garden would proceed exactly as planned and that the builders would arrive in the autumn. Edith read it twice, and the second time she read it more slowly, as she had once read the worst of her pupils' essays.

The residents crowded around the board and read the notice with growing anger, and the murmur in the hall rose until it sounded like wind in the trees. Gwen tapped her stick on the floorboards, and somebody at the back said that it was a disgrace to sell a dead man's garden before he was even buried. Stott had already vanished into his office, closing the door with a polite and cowardly click.

Edith stood apart from the crowd, tapping her pencil against her lip, with her eyes fixed on the white notice. If Stott had known about the letter, she reasoned, he would hardly have been so quick to announce the sale, and so either he had never seen it or he was a much better actor than she had supposed. She decided that the first possibility was kinder and the second more likely, and she wrote them both down.

That afternoon a small grey car crunched up the drive, and a tired woman in a dark coat stepped out and stood looking up at the house. She was Ruth Vane, Conrad's sister, and she had driven for six hours without stopping to eat. She had her brother's sharp chin and his cool grey eyes, but her mouth was softer, and there were fresh tears on her cheeks.

Edith offered to show Ruth the garden, and the two women walked slowly along the rose walk side by side. Ruth admitted, in a voice that she tried to keep steady, that she had not spoken to her brother for a year because they had quarrelled bitterly over money. When she reached the last of the roses she stopped and put a hand to her mouth, because the pink bloom in front of her was her brother's favourite colour.

Soon afterwards a heavy red-faced man with rolled plans under his arm strode into the hall and demanded in a loud voice to see Mr Stott at once. He was Dennis Kemp of Kemp and Sons, the builders who had agreed to buy the garden, and he had the impatient air of a man who is used to being obeyed. Fergus, who happened to be mending a cupboard handle in the hall, found that he could hear every word.

Fergus overheard Kemp complaining, in a voice that carried across the hall, that his money had been ready since Monday and that he had been solemnly promised the garden. Stott soothed him in a low and oily voice, saying that Mr Vane's sad death changed nothing and that the sale would be completed within the month. Kemp grunted, tucked his plans under his arm like a sulky schoolboy and stamped out to his van.

That evening Edith added two more names to the list in her notebook, with the sigh of a woman who dislikes suspecting people. Dennis Kemp would lose a great deal of money if the sale failed, and Ruth Vane, as her brother's only relative, would inherit Maple Court and everything in it. People had done terrible things for less, she reflected, and she did not enjoy having to remember it.

Edith drew a careful table with three columns: those who wanted the sale to go ahead, those who wanted it stopped, and those who could reach a key to the glasshouse. The names crossed from one column to another in surprising places, and she frowned at the page for the best part of an hour. At the end of it she had learned one useful thing, which was how much she still did not know.

At the next Wednesday meeting Edith asked whether the club wished to continue, since the work was proving far harder than any newspaper puzzle and rather more frightening. Every hand went up before she had finished the question, and Lucy, who had been listening at the door with a tray, brought in the lemon cake as though she had been waiting all week to do so. It was not a celebration exactly, but it was certainly a promise, and nobody at the table mistook it for anything else.

Gwen's eyes were tired, and she had never trusted numbers, so she asked Meera to help her with a bank statement that had arrived that morning. They sat together in Gwen's little sitting room under the reading lamp, with a pot of tea and a plate of ginger biscuits between them. Outside the window the roses nodded in the breeze, and the afternoon seemed as calm as any afternoon could be.

Meera ran her finger down the page and then stopped, because something had snagged on her nurse's habit of noticing small things. The care fee appeared twice in every month, once under its proper name and once under a slightly different heading that was very easy to overlook. She looked back through three earlier statements and found the same pattern, month after month, as regular as a clock.

Gwen said that she had always supposed that was how care fees worked, because nobody had ever explained them to her and she had been too proud to ask. Meera told her gently that the contract named one fee only and nothing more, and that the page should be kept somewhere very safe. Gwen put it inside her favourite recipe book, which she considered the safest place in the building.

Meera and Fergus went from door to door along the upstairs corridor with a notebook and a plate of Lucy's biscuits, which Fergus described as a bribe in a good cause. They asked the residents very politely whether they would let them look at their monthly statements, and they promised to say nothing to anyone. Most of the residents agreed at once, because it was a pleasure to be asked about anything by somebody who listened.

Ravi Anand, a retired bus conductor with a wonderful memory for tickets, was the first to open his door, and Tilly Drummond, who never stopped knitting, was the second. Their statements showed exactly the same pair of lines in every month, one proper and one extra, and Mr Anand put on his glasses to be sure that he was not imagining it. He was not imagining it, and his cheerful face became very grave indeed as he handed the page back.

By the end of the afternoon they had seen eleven statements, and every one of them showed the extra fee in the same slightly disguised words. Each resident had been paying the same fee twice over every single month, a sum that nobody had questioned, which added up across the whole house to something very large indeed. Meera wrote the total at the bottom of the page and then sat quite still for a moment.

Meera looked back through the older statements that the residents kept in biscuit tins and shoeboxes, and she saw that the extra fee had started about a year before. Until that month every resident had paid exactly the right amount, and from the moment the new company took over the accounts every one of them had paid twice. Somebody, she said in a low voice, had changed something at Maple Court, and had been counting on nobody to look.

Meera brought the figures to Edith, who listened without a word and then closed her notebook very gently. Someone had been taking money from the residents for a year, she said, and the person who looked after the billing for the whole house was the finance manager. She warned her friends that they must be careful, because a suspicion is not a fact and a man's good name is not a toy.

Gwen reminded them, tapping her stick for emphasis, that Mr Vane had read her crumpled paper at the fair and had gone as quiet as a stone. He had folded it into his inside pocket, she said, and she had not seen it since, and she had thought him rather rude at the time. Edith's pencil stopped in the middle of a word, and for a moment she did not breathe at all.

Edith wrote two words on a clean page and underlined them twice: Vane knew. If Mr Vane had understood the extra fees on Saturday afternoon, she reasoned, it might explain both the change in his heart and the meeting that he had arranged for nine o'clock that night. Somebody had a very good reason to keep him quiet before Monday, and the question was who had learned that he knew.

A few mornings later Edith watched Harold Stott cross the hall in his gleaming black shoes, walking with the brisk bounce of a man who has nothing on his conscience. In the slanting light from the window she saw a thin line of red dust along the edge of one sole, as fine as flour on a baker's sleeve. It was the only untidy thing about him, and that alone made it interesting.

Everybody at Maple Court knew that Stott polished his shoes every morning with a brush and a little tin of black wax, because Lucy had once found him doing it in the kitchen. If there was red dust on them now, Edith reasoned, it had come from somewhere that very day or the day before, since he would have wiped it away otherwise. She wondered where in Willowby anyone could find red dust, and the answer came to her at once.

Edith stopped him in the hall and asked, as though it were of no importance, whether he had been walking in the garden that week. Stott replied with a hearty laugh that he had not set foot in it since the fair, because gardens gave him hay fever and he preferred his office. His eyes dropped for a moment to his shoes and rose again very quickly.

That afternoon Edith walked every path of the garden with her eyes on the ground, like a woman looking for a dropped ring. She found grey gravel and green lawn and brown flowerbeds, but not one grain of red dust anywhere outside the glasshouse. If Stott had red clay on his shoes, she concluded, then he had been inside that building, and he had been there recently.

Walter put on his best station cap and marched to Willowby railway station to see for himself, for he trusted a printed notice more than any man's memory. The board by the ticket office still carried a large yellow poster announcing that no trains would run between Willowby and the city on the Saturday and Sunday of the fair. Walter read it twice with deep satisfaction, which was not a feeling that he often had at stations.

The stationmaster, Mr Greaves, remembered Walter from the old days and was delighted to talk to a fellow railwayman. He confirmed that not one train had left Willowby station on Saturday, from the first light of morning to the last of the night, and that every traveller had gone by replacement bus. He added that he had been so bored that he had counted the passengers, and that there had been eleven in the whole day.

Mr Greaves showed Walter the replacement timetable, which he kept pinned inside his office door like a treasured certificate. The only bus to the city that evening left from outside the station at twenty past six, he said, and the next one did not go until nearly eleven o'clock. Anyone who had truly left Maple Court at six would have caught that bus, he added, because there was nothing else to catch.

Walter tracked down the driver of the six-twenty bus, a cheerful woman called Nina Doyle, who was drinking tea beside her parked bus in a jacket of astonishing yellow. She had carried only six passengers that evening, she said, two students, a woman with a dog and three tourists, and not one of them had been a round, rosy man in a good suit. She would certainly have remembered him, she added, because rosy men in good suits tipped nobody and complained about everything.

Walter walked home slowly, writing down everything he had learned on the back of a bus ticket, because a railwayman never trusts his memory with anything important. A man who claims to have taken a train that did not run, he told himself, is either hopelessly confused or deliberately lying, and Harold Stott had never looked confused in his life. The thought sat in his chest all the way home like a heavy dinner.

That evening Walter laid his bus ticket on the table in the Garden Room and told the others everything that he had found. Edith said quietly that Stott had lied about the train, and that the most natural reason for such a lie was that he had never left Maple Court at all. Nobody laughed at this, nobody spoke for a while, and the clock on the mantelpiece ticked very loudly in the silence.

Fergus asked Joe whether he might look again, more carefully this time, at the grey cabinet and the spare key inside it. Joe opened it with his broad back turned, as before, and Sergeant Rudd, who happened to be passing the door, said that he would allow it as long as nothing was removed. Fergus put on a pair of white cotton gloves that he had brought from his flat, and he looked very serious indeed.

Fergus studied the keypad through his lens and smiled with a craftsman's pleasure, because the old buttons told their own story. Four of the ten were polished by use and dull around the edges, and the others were as clean and crisp as the day they were fitted. It meant that very few people used the cabinet, he explained, and that they used it often.

Fergus lifted the spare key by its paper tag and tilted it toward the window, and the light picked out something that nobody else would have seen. In the creases of the paper and in the little ring of the key there was a trace of fine red dust, as bright as brick powder and quite unmistakable. Joe stared at it, then at Fergus, and then began to mutter something that was probably not polite.

Fergus explained that red clay dust was found nowhere but in the glasshouse, so the person who had used the key must have touched the red pots only a minute before. The dust had passed from his hands to the key, and he had returned it to the cabinet without noticing, exactly as a clever person does when he is frightened and in a hurry. Fergus had known locks for fifty years, and he had never yet met a hurried criminal who remembered to wash his hands.

They asked Lucy who knew the code of the cabinet, and she answered at once with her chin in the air, because she knew precisely how it must sound. Only three people knew it, she said, which were Joe, Mr Stott and herself, and Mr Vane had never learned it. She did not add that she was frightened, but her hands, which twisted at her apron, said it for her.

Lucy swore on her mother's recipe book that she had not touched the key. She had served supper until half past eight, she said, and then she had sat in the lounge with a dozen residents, watching an old film and eating the leftover cake, until ten o'clock. Mr Anand, who had been one of them, nodded firmly and said that every word of it was true.

Joe scratched his head and said that he had no reason to touch the cabinet on Saturday, since he already carried a key of his own on his belt. Besides, he had been at his daughter's house all evening, losing at cards to a ten-year-old, and Pat and Sam were ready to swear to it before any judge in the land. Edith believed him, and Sergeant Rudd, who had telephoned Pat that morning, believed him too.

Edith crossed Lucy and Joe off her list for the night in question, because both of them had witnesses and both had told the truth. That left only Harold Stott, who knew the code, who had lied about his train, and who had red dust on his shoes. The three facts lined up in her mind like buttons on a coat, but she knew that a row of buttons is not the same as a coat.

Fergus walked the whole length of the garden and found a green gate hidden behind an overgrown rose bush at the very bottom. It opened from the lane with a simple latch and no key at all, and it swung wide without a sound. A man who had signed out at the front door could therefore have walked back in through the garden without a single person seeing him.

Edith stood at the green gate and looked up the dusky garden toward the glasshouse, which glowed faintly in the last of the light. A man could have come in that way unseen, she said, but a possibility was not proof, and it was proof that the sergeant would need. She turned back toward the house with her three friends, thinking how much easier mysteries were in newspapers, where the answer was always printed upside down at the bottom of the page.

At the next Wednesday meeting Sergeant Rudd sat down among the four friends with a slice of lemon cake balanced on his knee and his notebook beside his boots. He had come, he said, because Edith had asked him very politely, and in all his twenty-six years nobody had ever refused her successfully. The members of the club nodded gravely, because that was exactly what Edith's former pupils had always said.

Edith counted off the clues on her fingers, beginning with the lie about the train, the red dust on Stott's shoes and the double fees on eleven statements. She finished with the dusty spare key and with Gwen's man in the long raincoat, and when she had done she folded her hands in her lap like a teacher who has just given an excellent lesson. The sergeant had stopped chewing some time before, and his cake lay forgotten and untouched upon his knee.

The sergeant thought it over carefully and then shook his head with real regret. Stott could say that he had visited the glasshouse earlier in the week, he pointed out, and a bus driver might easily forget a face, and a lie about a train was only a lie. A court would want something that could not be explained away, and so far the friends had nothing but a handful of excellent suspicions.

Sergeant Rudd explained, with a sigh, that Inspector Hale considered the matter closed, and that the inspector disliked changing his mind almost as much as he disliked working on Sundays. Without something solid in his hand, Rudd said, he could not even ask for permission to search an office, let alone to arrest a finance manager. He looked miserable, and Meera pressed a second slice of cake on him out of sheer kindness.

What he needed, said Rudd, leaning forward across the tea table, was a confession, or something very close to one. If Stott could be tricked into uttering a detail that only the person who had stood in the glasshouse could possibly know, then the inspector would be compelled to listen. The four friends exchanged glances, and each of them reached the same conclusion, though only one of them already held the means of doing it.

Edith said nothing aloud, but in her mind she was turning over the secret that the sergeant had told her on the steps. Only the killer, the sergeant, the doctor and Joe knew about the shelf of pots that had been pulled down, and none of them would ever mention it by mistake. If somebody else should mention it, she thought, that would be a different matter entirely.

Edith proposed a residents' meeting for the Thursday of the following week, at which Stott would be asked to speak about the sale as the manager of the house. She would speak afterwards, she said, and she would tell the sad news of Mr Vane very carefully and very plainly, and then wait to see what Stott said in reply. It was not so much a plan as a fishing trip, she admitted, but it was the best that she could do.

Edith drew a plan in her notebook with four small circles for the friends and one large cross for Stott in the middle of the page. Every circle had a job to do, and each job was written beside it in her tidiest teacher's handwriting, with arrows to show who should speak first. The sergeant studied the plan for a long time and then said, with a smile, that it was better organised than most police operations.

Rudd agreed to wait in the next room with the door open a crack, ready to step in at a word from Edith, and he promised not to eat any more cake until the matter was over. Joe, who was to stand at the back of the lounge with his arms folded, would say nothing unless somebody spoke his name. Everyone had a place and everyone had a part, and the whole thing hung by a single thread of Stott's pride.

That night Edith sat at her window with a cup of mint tea and watched the dark shape of the glasshouse at the end of the garden. She had never been so nervous before a lesson, and she had taught thousands of them, to children who were far more alarming than Harold Stott. At last she went to bed, and she slept better than she had expected.

On Wednesday afternoon the friends set out rows of chairs in the Garden Room exactly as they would stand in the lounge on the following morning. Edith took the part of the speaker, Joe's empty chair stood at the back, and Meera moved from seat to seat to play the whole crowd of residents. It was such a peculiar sight that Lucy, who looked in with a tray, retreated without a word.

Walter practised his part about the train, but he began with the invention of the steam engine and had reached the Great Western Railway before Edith took his card away. She drew a firm line through nine tenths of it and gave it back, with the remark that the residents wanted a fact and not a lecture. Walter sulked magnificently for almost a minute and then read it again, in four sentences.

Meera practised her part, which was to hold up the statements and explain the double fees to the whole room in a quiet and steady voice. Her hands shook a little at first, so Fergus lent her a clipboard to hold, and she found that a clipboard made her feel as authoritative as a consultant. By the third attempt she could have read the figures to a lion without a tremor.

Fergus practised holding up a stand-in key and delivering his lines, and on the very first attempt the key slid out of his gnarled fingers and struck the floor with a clatter. For the first time in three weeks the whole club burst out laughing, and the sound was so welcome that nobody wanted it to stop. Fergus picked up the key with great dignity and said that the real one would be held much more firmly.

Gwen heard about the plan from Edith, who had decided that she was far too sharp to be left out, and she insisted on a seat in the front row. She announced that she would tap her stick on the floor whenever she heard a lie, and Edith begged her, with great politeness and some alarm, to do nothing of the kind. Gwen agreed to tap only once, at the most important moment, and she would not be argued out of it.

Lucy had been told only that there would be an important meeting, and she baked a lemon cake for it without being asked. Nobody was ever brave on an empty stomach, she said, and the smell of lemon and sugar drifted through the corridors of Maple Court until half the residents had decided to come early. It was the nearest thing to a flag of truce that the house possessed.

Edith told Ruth Vane just enough of the plan to win her trust and not a word more, and Ruth agreed to come and sit in the front row beside Gwen. She promised to keep her face still whatever she heard, and since her brother's face had been famous for staying still, Edith believed that she would manage. Ruth asked only one question, which was whether the garden would be safe, and Edith answered that she hoped so with all her heart.

Joe grumbled that he was a gardener and not an actor, but in the end he agreed to stand at the back of the lounge with his arms folded. He would say nothing, he promised, unless Edith put a question to him, and even then he would say as little as the truth allowed. Edith assured him that this was exactly what she required, and that he was the best man in Willowby for the part.

On Wednesday evening Edith left her notebook on a table in the hall for no more than a moment, and Harold Stott picked it up with a polite smile and a bright, interested eye. She took it gently out of his hand and told him sweetly that it was only her shopping list, and that she was afraid she had run out of biscuits again. Stott laughed, but he did not stop watching her until she had gone out of sight.

On the night before the meeting Edith walked down the garden in the moonlight and stood at the door of the glasshouse for a long time. Inside, the tomatoes were ripening in the dark, as they had ripened on the night that Conrad Vane died, and she felt strangely calm. Tomorrow, she told the sleeping roses quietly, somebody was going to say something that he should not.

On Thursday morning the lounge slowly filled with residents, who carried their own cushions and cups of tea and talked in low, excited voices. By ten o'clock every chair was taken, the lemon cake stood on a long table under a white cloth, and the room hummed like a hive at the end of a warm day. Edith sat in the second row with her notebook closed on her knee and her heart beating faster than she liked.

Harold Stott arrived at five minutes past ten, smiling broadly and carrying his briefcase in front of him like a tray of drinks. His shoes shone brighter than ever, and he took his place at the front of the lounge with the easy confidence of a man who has never once been caught. Edith looked down at her notebook and then, very slowly and with a steady heart, she looked up again.

Sergeant Rudd had slipped into the little sitting room next door before anyone arrived, and he sat there on a hard chair with a very straight back. He had left the door open exactly the width of a notebook, and through the gap he could see Stott's shoulder and hear every breath in the lounge. He had never been so nervous in his life, and he had arrested a man for stealing a bicycle only last week.

Stott rose, spread his hands wide and spoke to the residents in his warm and well-oiled voice. He was extremely sorry, he said, but the sale of the garden must go ahead in accordance with the late Mr Vane's wishes, and the builders would arrive in the autumn. He used the word unfortunately four times in a single minute, and he seemed rather pleased with it each time.

A long groan rolled around the room, and somebody at the back called out that it was a shame and a disgrace. Gwen held her stick in both hands and did not tap it once, though it was plain from the set of her jaw that it cost her a great deal. Ruth Vane, sitting beside her, laid a gentle hand over Gwen's knuckles and said nothing.

Edith rose from her seat in the second row and asked, with her best classroom politeness, whether she might say a few words. Stott waved a gracious hand and told her that of course she might, since she was without doubt the wisest member of the house. Edith thanked him with a smile that would have chilled a more perceptive man.

Edith spoke quietly and simply to the whole room, and the residents leaned forward to catch her words. She reminded them that Mr Vane had been found on a Sunday morning in the locked glasshouse after what the police had called a fall, and that nobody had explained why he had gone there so late at night. She said nothing about shelves, or pots, or the back of his head, and she watched Stott's face as she spoke.

Stott shook his head, dabbed his brow and sighed with great feeling, like a man who was determined to be helpful. Poor Mr Vane, he murmured, lying there on the floor under all those pots that somebody had pulled down on top of him, it was too dreadful to imagine. The words were out of his mouth before his good sense could catch them, and they hung in the air of the lounge like a dropped plate.

A silence fell over the lounge so complete that people could hear the clock on the mantelpiece and the breathing of their neighbours. Then Gwen, who had promised to tap exactly once, brought her stick down on the floorboards with a single clear crack, like a judge's gavel. Stott started and looked about him, and for the first time that morning he did not smile.

Edith turned to face him and asked, quietly and almost kindly, how he knew that the pots had been pulled down on top of Mr Vane. Nobody at Maple Court had been told that, she said, not the residents, not the staff and certainly not the finance manager, who had been far away in London. Every head in the room swung toward Stott, and the lounge became as still as a photograph.

Stott went pale beneath his rosy cheeks, and his smile slid sideways like a picture hung crooked. He said, rather too quickly, that somebody must have told him, and that he rather thought it had been Joe the gardener, though he could not recall the occasion. A bead of sweat travelled slowly down his temple, and the whole room watched it go.

Joe unfolded his arms at the back of the room and said, in his gruffest voice, that he had told nobody at all. He had spoken of it only to the sergeant, he said, in the glasshouse with the door shut, and he had not so much as whispered it to his own daughter. His voice shook a little with anger, which was more convincing than any speech.

Stott tried again, with a nervous laugh, and said that perhaps it had been Lucy who had told him. Lucy, who was standing at the door with a tea tray in her hands, said in a small and perfectly clear voice that she had never even seen the pots, and that nobody had ever mentioned them to her. The tray rattled on its cups once, and then it was quite still again in her steady hands.

Walter stood up in the third row holding a yellow railway notice that Mr Greaves had lent him, and the whole room turned to look. He announced, in the voice of a man who had once stopped express trains, that he had a small question about the six-fifteen to London. There had not been a six-fifteen on that Saturday, he said, nor a six-twenty, nor any train at all, because the line was closed for repairs, exactly as the large black letters of his notice declared.

Stott swallowed twice and said that of course he had taken the replacement bus, and that he had simply used the word train out of habit, as everyone did. It was an easy mistake, he said, and nobody should be blamed for it, and he gave a short high laugh that nobody joined. Edith noted that for a man who had just been caught in a lie, he was extraordinarily quick to find a second one.

Walter said calmly that the only replacement bus had left at twenty past six, and that its driver, Nina Doyle, remembered every one of her six passengers. None of them had been a round, rosy man in a good suit, she had told him, because she would never have forgotten a man who complained so much. A ripple of laughter went through the room, and it was not a kind one.

Meera rose from her chair with her clipboard held in front of her and said, in her calm nurse's voice, that eleven residents had been charged their care fee twice every month for a whole year. She asked Mr Stott, as the manager of the accounts, whether he would be kind enough to explain how such a thing could happen. The residents who had given her their statements held them up one by one, like a field of white flags.

Stott replied hurriedly that it was merely an accounting error and that he would put it right at once, with a full apology to everybody concerned. His voice had risen half an octave, however, and a small muscle had begun to twitch in his cheek. Mr Anand, who had spent forty years counting tickets and spotting people who cheated on them, said loudly that it was a very peculiar error that happened to benefit only one person.

Fergus stood up very slowly and held the spare glasshouse key high above his head, so that the red dust in its paper tag caught the light from the window. Only three people knew the code of the cabinet in which it lived, he said in his steadiest voice, and one of the three had told everybody that he had been on a train. The key did not shake in his hand at all, and he thought with quiet pride of the stand-in that he had dropped in rehearsal.

Harold Stott looked around the room at the faces of the people he had robbed, and not a single one of them was smiling back. The round face that had always been so cheerful and so rosy slowly turned the colour of old paper, and the shoes that he had polished so lovingly seemed suddenly to be the only part of him that still shone. His mouth opened, and for a moment nothing came out of it at all.

Harold Stott's knees gave way beneath him, and he sank into the nearest armchair with his head in his hands and his polished shoes turned inward. The whole room waited without a sound, and nobody offered him a handkerchief, though it was noticed that his own stayed in his pocket. When at last he spoke, his voice was small and hoarse, and it did not sound at all like the voice of the manager.

He said that he had taken the money from the residents, a little at a time, over the whole of the last year. He had borrowed far more than he could repay, he said to the carpet, and he had told himself every month that he would put it all back before anyone noticed. A second line on a bill, he whispered, had seemed such a small and quiet thing to add.

Mr Vane had seen Gwen's crumpled bank paper at the fair, Stott said, and he had understood the whole scheme in less than a minute. That afternoon he had taken Stott aside behind the tea tent, very quietly and without a smile, and told him to bring the account books to the glasshouse at nine o'clock that night. Gwen, who was listening with her mouth open, drew in a long and very audible breath.

He had signed out at six o'clock on purpose, he admitted, so that everyone would believe he was safely on the way to London. Then he had parked his silver car in the lane behind the church and waited for the dark, with his long raincoat buttoned over his good suit, because a white shirt shows in a garden at night. It had been the longest wait of his life, and he had spent it eating mints.

When it was nearly dark he had walked back through the green gate at the bottom of the garden, which nobody ever thought to watch. He had slipped into the estate office by the garden door, tapped in the code that he had known for a year and taken the spare key from its brass hook while the residents laughed at an old film. Even now, he said bitterly, he could not believe how easy it had been.

Mr Vane had been waiting for him at the potting bench, Stott said, with a pile of account books and a tired but steady face. He had told Stott quietly that the sale was cancelled, that every pound must be repaid and that the police would be told on Monday, though he had added that he was sorry that it had come to this. It was the kindness that Stott could not bear, and he said so with a kind of astonishment.

In one moment of terrible panic, Stott said, he had picked up a heavy clay pot from the shelf and struck Mr Vane once from behind while Mr Vane was bending over the account books. Mr Vane had fallen without a sound and had never moved again, and Stott had stood looking at the pot in his own hand for what seemed like an hour. Meera closed her eyes, and so did several others, because even the gentlest listener has a limit to what she can bear.

Then, Stott said, with the cold calm of a man who had already done the worst thing of his life, he had pulled a whole shelf of red pots down over Mr Vane. It would look like a dreadful accident, he had thought, and he had thought it very clever at the time, and the red dust from the broken clay had settled on his hands and shoes without his noticing. Edith, who knew exactly what that dust had told them, closed her notebook with a quiet click.

He had pushed the spare key into the lock with trembling fingers, Stott said, and he had scratched the brass around it in his haste. Then he had put the key back in the cabinet, taken the account books from the bench and Gwen's paper from the dead man's pocket, and left the lamp burning, because in his terror he had forgotten that lamps exist. He had never known about the letter in the seed tin, and he had never thought of looking there.

When he had finished, nobody in the lounge said a word, and Gwen's stick lay forgotten on the floor where it had fallen. Edith had expected to feel proud of herself, but she felt only a heavy sadness for Conrad Vane, who had changed his mind a few hours too late. She laid her notebook on her knee, and for the first time in thirty years she could think of nothing at all to write.

Sergeant Rudd stepped through the door of the little room next door, where he had heard every word of the confession. He took Stott gently by the arm, and in a formal voice that shook only a very little he told him that he was under arrest for the death of Conrad Vane and for the theft of the residents' money. Stott did not struggle and did not speak, and he got to his feet like a man who was glad that it was over.

Stott was led out through the hall, and his polished shoes clicked on the tiles with a sound that everybody in the building would remember for years. The residents stood in a silent line on either side, and a police car that had been waiting in the drive opened its door for him. Not until it had driven away down the avenue did anyone dare to breathe out.

Sergeant Rudd shook Edith's hand, and then the hands of Walter, Meera and Fergus, with an unsteady smile of pure relief. Inspector Hale would be changing his mind that very afternoon, he said, and would not enjoy it in the least, but the case would now be in a proper file. Joe, standing at the back of the lounge, wiped his eyes with the back of his hand and pretended that it was hay fever.

The police searched Stott's tidy office and his silver car, and what they found left no room for argument. In the boot lay the missing account books, bundled in a carrier bag as though they were laundry, and on the hook behind the office door hung the long fawn raincoat with red clay still dusting its sleeves. Gwen, informed of the discovery, remarked that she had always known there was something wrong with a man who polished his shoes every day.

Over the following weeks the police and a patient accountant followed the stolen money through four bank accounts, and by the end of the summer they had found most of it. Ruth Vane made up the rest from her brother's estate without being asked, saying quietly that it was exactly what Conrad would have wanted. Not one resident lost a single pound, and the eleven statements were corrected line by line.

One bright morning eleven residents opened eleven identical envelopes at the breakfast table and found their money returned to the last penny. Ravi Anand laughed so loudly that the cutlery rattled, Tilly Drummond dropped a stitch for the first time in twenty years, and Gwen wept happily into her tea. Lucy, who had baked a celebration cake for the occasion, wept a little too, mostly out of sympathy.

As her brother's only family, Ruth Vane now owned Maple Court, and Sergeant Rudd brought her Conrad's letter from the police safe in a clean envelope. She read it three times, standing very still by the window, and when she reached the line about money not being the only thing worth owning she had to sit down. She had not forgiven herself for their year of silence, but the letter made the weight of it a little lighter.

Ruth signed a legal paper in the Garden Room, with all four friends as witnesses, saying that the garden of Maple Court would never be sold to anyone. Dennis Kemp read it through with a face as sour as a lemon, rolled up his plans with a sigh and drove away to look for some other field to spoil. Fergus, who had never witnessed anything so important, signed his name with his tongue between his teeth.

Ruth told Joe that he would be the head gardener of Maple Court for as long as he wished, with a better wage and a proper hut for his tools. She also gave him a new wheelbarrow with a blue bow on its handle, and Joe, who had not smiled in public for twenty years, very nearly did. He said that it was a decent barrow and wheeled it away at once before anybody could see his face.

Gwen chose a new rose of the palest pink, the colour that Conrad Vane had loved, and planted it beside the glasshouse with her own hands on a folded cushion. Joe dug the hole and Ruth poured the first can of water, and the old gardener and the old lady agreed for once on every point. Gwen patted the earth flat and told the little bush, in a firm voice, that it was now part of the family.

On the following Sunday the residents gathered by the glasshouse in their best clothes to remember Conrad Vane, a man most of them had known for only a week and understood only at the end. Ruth spoke a few simple words about her brother, and Edith read aloud the last lines of his letter in a clear and steady voice. The sun came out as she finished, and it was agreed afterwards that this was a coincidence of the very best sort.

Ruth asked Joe to show her how to plant the tomato seeds from the old seed tin, and the two of them knelt together on the glasshouse floor with a tray of damp earth between them. The air began to smell of fresh soil and water again, and slowly the glasshouse began to seem a happy place instead of a sad one. Joe corrected her grip on the seedling without a word of unkindness, which Edith, watching from the door, noted as a small miracle.

In the Garden Room the four friends sank into their armchairs and talked for a long time about everything that they had done. They had solved a real case, Fergus said, with real consequences, and not one of them could quite believe that it had been done with a lock, a timetable, a notebook and a nurse's eye. Walter said that it was the best-run operation he had ever taken part in, apart from the great timetable change of nineteen seventy-four.

That evening Edith opened a fresh notebook and wrote the date at the top of a clean page, as she had done at the start of every school year for thirty years. She had never expected to need another notebook for such a purpose, and she was surprised by how much she hoped that she would. Beneath the date she wrote a single word, which was begin, and she underlined it twice with a firm and steady pencil.

At the next meeting Lucy carried in a lemon cake with a single candle burning in the middle of it, and she set it on the table with a ceremonial flourish. She said that it was a thank-you to the Wednesday Club from the whole kitchen, and then she blew her nose loudly before anybody could remark on the state of her eyes. The cake was eaten to the last crumb, and a second one was demanded before the plates had even been cleared away.

A week later Sergeant Rudd appeared at the door of the Garden Room with a box of cakes in one hand and a thick brown folder in the other, looking like a boy who has come to ask a favour. He cleared his throat and asked, rather shyly, whether the club might consider helping him with another puzzle. He had learned, he said, that the police could solve most things, but that the Wednesday Club could solve the ones that mattered.

Rudd opened the folder on the table, and four heads leaned over it at once, like sunflowers turning toward the light. Inside lay a puzzle from the town of Willowby itself, the tale of a rare old book that had vanished from the library twenty years before and had never been found. Nobody had ever been blamed, he said, and nobody had ever been quite forgiven either.

Walter declared that he would check every date in the library records, and Fergus announced that he wished to inspect all the locks in the building, whether they had been involved or not. Meera promised to talk to the retired librarians, who she suspected would be delighted to be asked, and Edith turned to a new page and began her list. By the time the second pot of tea arrived, the club had already divided the case into four parts and the cake into five.

As the afternoon turned to evening, the four friends carried their tea out into the garden and sat among the roses, with Sergeant Rudd on a stool beside them and a plate of cake on every knee. Gwen's new pink rose stood beside the glasshouse, still thin and green, and yet it already looked as if it had always belonged there. Somewhere beyond the hedge a blackbird was singing the last song of the day.

In the long gold light of the evening the four friends sat among the roses with their tea, and the glasshouse glowed behind them like a lantern. The trouble was over, the thief was caught, and the garden would belong to Maple Court for as long as anyone could imagine, while Sergeant Rudd's folder lay unopened on Edith's knee. Edith smiled at her three friends and said that there was no hurry, because the best puzzles, like the best cakes, were meant to be shared.
